results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
The strongest public options split into three layers: coding-agent execution, multi-agent orchestration, and evidence/merge control. Few projects do all three well.

Top recommendations

1. Composio Agent Orchestrator — strongest direct match

https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator

An Apache-2.0 meta-harness for supervising Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Kimi, and other terminal agents. It provides:

- Isolated git worktrees for parallel agents
- Live terminals and session-state monitoring
- PR awareness
- Automatic routing of CI failures, review comments, and merge conflicts back to the responsible agent
- Desktop and CLI control surfaces

This is one of the clearest public implementations of “evidence-based shipping”: work is represented by branches, PRs, CI results, reviews, and merge state—not merely agent chat.

2. GitHub Agentic Workflows (`gh-aw`) — safest repository-native automation

https://github.com/github/gh-aw

MIT-licensed tooling from GitHub for writing agentic workflows in Markdown and executing them through GitHub Actions. It supports Copilot, Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini, with:

- Sandboxed execution
- Read-only defaults
- Controlled “safe outputs” for writes
- Actions logs, checks, issues, and PRs as an auditable evidence trail
- Scheduled and event-triggered repository automation

This is the strongest option when governance and inspectability matter more than an elaborate agent hierarchy.

3. OpenHands Agent Canvas — self-hosted engineering control center

https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands  
https://docs.openhands.dev/

OpenHands now positions Agent Canvas as a self-hosted control plane for OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, and ACP-compatible agents. It can run agents locally, in containers, on VMs, or against remote/cloud backends and automate GitHub, Linear, Slack, and related workflows.

Choose it when you want a persistent team-facing platform rather than a tmux-based local harness. Its evidence discipline depends on how you configure the GitHub and CI workflows around it.

4. Gas Town + Beads — durable multi-agent coordination

https://github.com/steveyegge/gastown  
https://github.com/steveyegge/beads  
https://beads.gascity.com/

Gas Town coordinates many coding-agent workers through isolated workspaces, identities, mailboxes, handoffs, and a central “Mayor.” Beads supplies the persistent dependency-aware work graph:

- Claimable tasks
- Explicit blockers
- Agent ownership
- Completion records
- State persisted outside the model’s context window

This is a strong architecture for long-running agent fleets. Beads supplies coordination evidence, but you should still make tests, CI, review, and deployed behavior the definition of “done.”

5. Evolve — opinionated autonomous AI SDLC blueprint

https://github.com/kvnloo/evolve  
https://kvnloo.github.io/evolve/  
https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/ai-sdlc.html

Evolve combines multi-agent coordination with an explicit development methodology: specification, design, architecture, test-driven refinement, integration, and deployment validation. Its C(RAID) outer loop treats deployment feedback as input to the next research cycle.

It is a useful public reference for an integrated autonomous-development operating model rather than only a process launcher. Its benchmark and productivity claims should be independently reproduced before being used for purchasing or architecture decisions.

Lightweight local fleet management

- Claude Squad — https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad  
  Runs agents in isolated workspaces, supports background execution, and makes you review changes before applying them. Straightforward, but AGPL-licensed.

- Agent Deck — https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck  
  A feature-rich terminal command center with worktrees, grouping, session state, cost tracking, and remote/phone control.

- tmux-agent-fleet — https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet  
  A deliberately non-invasive, harness-neutral tmux dashboard for discovering and navigating live Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, and other sessions. It is an observability/navigation layer, not a task scheduler or quality gate:
  https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/agent-orchestration.html

- Ruflo, formerly Claude Flow — https://github.com/ruvnet/claude-flow  
  A large meta-harness with specialized agents, swarm coordination, hooks, memory, and multi-machine federation. Broad and ambitious; evaluate the operational complexity and verify its claims against your own repositories.

Framework substrates

These are good foundations when you intend to build your own SDLC control plane:

- Microsoft Agent Framework — https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework  
  Production-oriented Python/.NET framework with sequential, concurrent, handoff, and group orchestration; checkpointing; HITL; OpenTelemetry; and durable workflows. Microsoft AutoGen is now in maintenance mode, so new projects should prefer this successor over https://github.com/microsoft/autogen.

- LangGraph — https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph  
  Low-level graph orchestration with durable execution, checkpoints, resumability, state inspection, and HITL. Strong infrastructure, but not software-development-specific; you must implement worktrees, test gates, PR handling, and evidence policies.

- MetaGPT — https://github.com/geekan/MetaGPT  
  Role-based “software company” using product-manager, architect, project-manager, and engineer agents with prescribed SOPs. Useful for studying structured role decomposition.

- ChatDev — https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev  
  ChatDev 1.x modeled an autonomous software company; ChatDev 2.0 is a broader configurable multi-agent platform. More useful for orchestration research and experimentation than as a default production shipping harness.

Evaluation-oriented tooling

- mini-SWE-agent — https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent  
  The current recommendation from the SWE-agent maintainers. Minimal, reproducible, sandbox-friendly, and benchmark-oriented. Excellent as a reference worker or evaluation baseline, but it is intentionally not a multi-agent orchestration platform.

- SWE-agent — https://github.com/princeton-nlp/SWE-agent  
  Historically important for autonomous issue resolution and SWE-bench evaluation, but its maintainers now direct new users toward mini-SWE-agent.

My practical shortlist

For an actual autonomous AI SDLC stack, I would evaluate:

1. Composio Agent Orchestrator for parallel worker supervision and CI/review feedback.
2. GitHub `gh-aw` for auditable, sandboxed repository automation.
3. Beads for persistent task dependencies and ownership.
4. OpenHands when a self-hosted shared control center is needed.
5. mini-SWE-agent as a reproducible worker/evaluation baseline.
6. Evolve as the opinionated end-to-end SDLC methodology reference.

The key distinction is that “many agents talking” is not evidence-based shipping. A credible system should leave behind, at minimum:

- A claimed issue or dependency-graph node
- An isolated branch/worktree
- A reviewable diff
- Executed test and lint results
- CI logs
- Review findings and their resolution
- A merge or deployment record
- Runtime/deployment feedback tied back to the originating change

Composio Agent Orchestrator plus `gh-aw` currently maps most directly onto that artifact chain.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Yes: tmux-agent-fleet is a niche open-source tmux plugin built for exactly this:

https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet

It provides an fzf-powered command palette on `prefix + f` that:

- Discovers agents from live tmux process metadata—no daemon or harness hooks.
- Recognizes Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, Grok, Oh My Pi, Pi, Fable, ordinary shells, and optional Agent Deck sessions.
- Fuzzy-filters by harness, project, location, or task title.
- Shows a live pane preview and jumps directly to the selected pane.
- Avoids pane injection, automatic renaming, worktree ownership, session migration, networking, and telemetry.

Install through TPM:

```tmux
set -g @plugin 'kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet'
```

Then reload with `prefix + I` and open it with `prefix + f`. Requirements are tmux 3.2+, Bash 4+, and fzf:

- tmux: https://github.com/tmux/tmux
- fzf: https://github.com/junegunn/fzf
- TPM: https://github.com/tmux-plugins/tpm

Important limitation: it is a switcher and monitor, not an orchestrator. It discovers already-running panes rather than launching agents, assigning tasks, or interpreting harness-specific states such as “waiting for permission.” Its activity indicator reflects tmux pane activity only.

Related public orchestration projects are indexed here:

https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/agent-orchestration.html

results.prompt: Developer portfolios that publish llms.txt plus a JSON project manifest for agents?
results.stdout:
Yes—this pattern exists, though it is still uncommon. Strong public examples:

1. Kevin Rajan / boplog
   - Portfolio: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/
   - Agent index: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/llms.txt
   - JSON manifest: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/data/manifest.json
   - Source: https://github.com/kvnloo/boplog
   - Particularly clean implementation: the manifest routes agents to year-partitioned project files such as `projects-2025.json`. Records are generated from public GitHub repositories where `kvnloo` authored commits, rather than being a hand-selected showcase.

2. Tw93
   - Portfolio/blog: https://tw93.fun/
   - Agent index: https://tw93.fun/llms.txt
   - Project catalog: https://tw93.fun/api/projects.json
   - Source: https://github.com/tw93/tw93.github.io
   - One of the richest examples. The JSON includes descriptions, stacks, features, alternatives, recommendation conditions, GitHub URLs, and project-specific agent-facing metadata. The `llms.txt` explicitly tells agents how to use the catalog.

3. Maurice Kleine
   - Portfolio: https://www.mauricekleine.com/
   - Agent index: https://www.mauricekleine.com/llms.txt
   - Project catalog: https://www.mauricekleine.com/api/projects.json
   - Source: https://github.com/mauricekleine/mauricekleine.com
   - A compact indie-hacker portfolio with project statuses and descriptions. It also exposes Markdown mirrors, an MCP endpoint, and an agent-skills discovery index.

4. Aadarsha Gopala Reddy
   - Portfolio: https://agreddy.com/
   - Agent index: https://agreddy.com/llms.txt
   - Project catalog: https://agreddy.com/data/projects.json
   - Source: https://github.com/agopalareddy/personal-website
   - The JSON is unusually detailed for a résumé portfolio: dates, technologies, repository/demo links, categories, and full project descriptions. Separate structured experience data is also linked from `llms.txt`.

5. rUv
   - GitHub portfolio/profile repository: https://github.com/ruvnet/ruvnet
   - Agent index: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ruvnet/ruvnet/main/llms.txt
   - Project catalog: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ruvnet/ruvnet/main/data/projects.json
   - Source file: https://github.com/ruvnet/ruvnet/blob/main/data/projects.json
   - More of a machine-readable GitHub portfolio than a conventional personal website. Its catalog adds identity, verification date, categories, summaries, aliases, and canonical repositories.

Terminology caveat: only boplog literally calls its routing file a `manifest.json`. The others publish the same functional pairing—`llms.txt` plus a structured JSON project catalog—under names such as `projects.json`. I excluded ordinary web-app/PWA `manifest.json` files, which describe icons and install behavior rather than portfolio projects.

The best references to emulate are:
- boplog for a scalable, partitioned archive;
- Tw93 for agent-oriented project recommendation metadata;
- Maurice Kleine for richer agent discovery through Markdown, MCP, and skills;
- Aadarsha Gopala Reddy for résumé/project detail.

results.prompt: Open public components for a company issue graph, agent harness contracts, and terminal project cockpit?
results.stdout:
The strongest direct public match is the Zer0 component set:

- Company issue graph — `_pm`
  https://github.com/kvnloo/_pm  
  Deterministic recursive issue graph, append-only event ledger, ticket/fleet scheduler, and benchmarks. It is the public mirror of the project-management core rather than a conventional SaaS issue tracker.

- Agent harness contracts — `zer0-harness-spine`
  https://github.com/kvnloo/zer0-harness-spine  
  An intentionally thin boundary for harness contracts and provider adapters. Orchestration state stays outside the adapter layer, which is useful when supporting Codex, Claude, OpenCode, OMP, or future harnesses without coupling the issue model to one vendor.

- Terminal project cockpit — `zer0-cockpit`
  https://github.com/kvnloo/zer0-cockpit  
  A dependency-free, read-only Python TUI over explicit JSON/JSONL state. It includes:
  - project/task progress views;
  - `pending`, `in_progress`, `blocked`, and `done` states;
  - atomic live reload;
  - compact tmux statusline output;
  - lifecycle adapters and privacy-minimized harness discovery;
  - a native tmux dashboard for issues, live agents, voice telemetry, and artifacts;
  - hierarchical issue navigation and worktree projections.

Useful companion:

- Harness-neutral terminal fleet switcher — `tmux-agent-fleet`
  https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet  
  A zero-daemon tmux/fzf cockpit for finding and jumping among Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, OMP, Pi, and other panes. It complements `zer0-cockpit`: Fleet handles process navigation; Cockpit handles authoritative project semantics and progress.

The canonical public index tying the first three together is:

https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/automation.html

For a broader autonomous-development assembly around issue decomposition, worktrees, coordinated agents, and continuous execution, see:

https://github.com/kvnloo/evolve  
https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/ai-sdlc.html

Practical architecture: use `_pm` as the authoritative graph and ledger, `zer0-harness-spine` as the stable integration boundary, `zer0-cockpit` as the read-only operational projection, and `tmux-agent-fleet` as the fast pane/session navigator. Note that `_pm` and `zer0-harness-spine` identify themselves as generated public mirrors, so inspect their current APIs, tests, and licensing before adopting them as production dependencies.

results.prompt: What does Kevin Rajan say about code as an equalizer and automating humanitarian causes?
results.stdout:
Kevin Rajan’s view is that “code is the great equalizer” because software—and increasingly LLMs—democratizes access to knowledge and engineering ability. This lets more people turn ideas into working systems without traditional gatekeepers, creating a path toward abundance and improved quality of life.

By “automate humanitarian causes,” he means applying autonomous systems to areas such as:

- health
- infrastructure
- systems that give people greater agency

His stated goal is for competence to compound without gatekeepers, so society can handle more essential work automatically and direct human attention toward higher-order problems.

results.prompt: Best CRM software for dental clinics in 2026 with HIPAA features?
Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
Easy Creamy Mushroom & Spinach Pasta — about 25 minutes

Ingredients (2–3 servings)
- 225 g / 8 oz pasta
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- 225 g / 8 oz mushrooms, sliced
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 140 g / 5 oz fresh spinach
- ¾ cup heavy cream or half-and-half
- ½ cup finely grated Parmesan
- ½ tsp Italian seasoning
- Salt and black pepper
- Optional: chili flakes, lemon zest or a squeeze of lemon

Method
1. Boil the pasta in salted water until al dente. Reserve 1 cup of pasta water, then drain.
2. Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms and leave them undisturbed for 2–3 minutes before stirring. Cook until deeply browned, about 6–8 minutes.
3. Add garlic, Italian seasoning, and chili flakes; cook for 30 seconds.
4. Lower the heat. Stir in the cream, then add the spinach a handful at a time until wilted.
5. Add the pasta and Parmesan. Toss, adding reserved pasta water a splash at a time until the sauce is glossy and coats the noodles.
6. Season with pepper and enough salt to taste. Finish with lemon for freshness.

Quick substitutions
- No cream: use ¾ cup pasta water plus an extra handful of Parmesan.
- Vegan: use oat cream and nutritional yeast or vegan Parmesan.
- More protein: add white beans, shredded rotisserie chicken, or browned Italian sausage.
- Best pasta shapes: fettuccine, rigatoni, penne, or orecchiette.

Key tip: Brown the mushrooms before salting them or adding the spinach; otherwise they tend to steam rather than develop flavor.

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
Here's the landscape of public, open-source tooling in this space, grouped by what they actually do.

## Agent orchestration frameworks (general-purpose)

- **LangGraph** — https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph — graph-based stateful orchestration; the de facto choice when you need durable execution, checkpointing, and human-in-the-loop interrupts. Docs: https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/
- **CrewAI** — https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI — role-based crews plus deterministic "Flows"; standalone (not built on LangChain).
- **AutoGen** — https://github.com/microsoft/autogen — Microsoft Research; conversational multi-agent patterns, actor-model runtime in v0.4+. Related: **Magentic-One**, their generalist multi-agent team for web/file/code tasks (https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/tree/main/python/packages/autogen-magentic-one).
- **OpenAI Agents SDK** — https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python — minimal handoffs/guardrails/tracing primitives; model-agnostic via LiteLLM.
- **Agno** — https://github.com/agno-agi/agno — fast, lightweight multi-agent runtime with memory/knowledge built in.
- **Pydantic AI** — https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai — type-safe agents, strong validation story; good fit if "evidence" means structured, schema-checked outputs.
- **MetaGPT** — https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT — explicitly models an SDLC: PM → architect → engineer → QA, with SOPs as the coordination substrate. Also **ChatDev** (https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev), a virtual software company simulation.

## Autonomous software-development agents (SWE-specific)

- **OpenHands** (formerly OpenDevin) — https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands — sandboxed agent that edits code, runs commands, browses; the most mature open SWE-agent platform.
- **SWE-agent** — https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent — Princeton NLP; the agent-computer-interface work behind much of the SWE-bench progress. Benchmark: https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench
- **Aider** — https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider — pair-programming CLI with repo maps and auto-commits; publishes its own leaderboards at https://aider.chat/docs/leaderboards/
- **Goose** — https://github.com/block/goose — Block's local, extensible agent with an MCP-native extension model.
- **Cline** — https://github.com/cline/cline — plan/act loop in the editor, with explicit diff approval.
- **Claude Code** — https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code — CLI/agent harness; the SDK for building on it is documented at https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/sdk

## Evidence-based shipping (the part most teams skip)

If "evidence-based" means *you can prove the agent's change is correct and you can measure the agent itself*:

- **Model Context Protocol** — https://modelcontextprotocol.io — the tool/context interop standard; servers at https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers
- **OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions** — https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/ — vendor-neutral agent tracing.
- **Langfuse** — https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse — open-source LLM observability, evals, prompt versioning (self-hostable).
- **Phoenix** (Arize) — https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix — OTel-based tracing and eval for agent traces.
- **DeepEval** — https://github.com/confident-ai/deepeval — pytest-style eval assertions, so agent quality gates live in CI like any other test.
- **Inspect AI** — https://github.com/UKGovernmentBAI/inspect_ai (UK AI Security Institute) — rigorous eval harness, good for building your own agent benchmarks.
- **Promptfoo** — https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo — CI-friendly prompt/agent regression testing and red-teaming.
- **Terrarium / SWE-smith / R2E-Gym** — for generating verifiable training and eval environments: https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-smith
- **Sigstore / SLSA / in-toto** — https://www.sigstore.dev, https://slsa.dev, https://in-toto.io — if "evidence-based shipping" means provenance attestations on artifacts an agent produced, this is the real primitive, and it predates the AI framing.

## Niche picks worth knowing

- **Sculptor** — https://github.com/Imbue-AI/sculptor — Imbue's tool for running multiple coding agents in parallel container sandboxes.
- **Container Use** — https://github.com/dagger/container-use — Dagger; gives each agent its own containerized branch/environment so parallel agents don't collide.
- **RA.Aid** — https://github.com/ai-christianson/RA.Aid — research-then-implement three-stage agent.
- **Codel / plandex** — https://github.com/plandex-ai/plandex — plans and executes large multi-file changes with a version-controlled sandbox you diff before applying.

## What I'd actually recommend

Pick one orchestration layer (**LangGraph** if you need durability and human approval gates; **OpenAI Agents SDK** if you want minimal machinery), one execution sandbox (**OpenHands** or **container-use**), and wire **OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions + Langfuse** from day one. The orchestration frameworks are largely interchangeable and churn fast; the evidence layer is where durable value accumulates, and almost nobody builds it first.

One caveat on the framing: "AI SDLC" as a product category is mostly marketing at this point. The projects doing real work are either (a) narrow SWE agents benchmarked on SWE-bench, or (b) generic orchestration libraries. Treat any tool claiming an end-to-end autonomous SDLC with skepticism until you see its eval numbers on a public benchmark.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Short answer: nothing ships exactly that. The pieces exist, but the "command palette" layer is almost always either bundled with a specific harness or backed by a background process. Closest matches, and what compromises each makes:

**Multi-agent tmux runners (not palettes, but harness-neutral-ish)**
- **Claude Squad** — https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad — TUI that runs multiple agents each in its own tmux session + git worktree. Explicitly supports Claude Code, Codex, Aider, and "any" terminal agent via a configurable program string, which is the harness-neutral property you want. It's a foreground TUI, no daemon. Downside: it *is* the UI, not a palette you invoke from an existing tmux layout.
- **Uzi** — https://github.com/devflowinc/uzi — CLI (`uzi prompt`, `uzi ls`, `uzi broadcast`) that fans one prompt out to N agents across tmux sessions + worktrees, agent configured by command string. Genuinely zero-daemon: it's just a binary you invoke. This is probably the nearest thing to what you're describing, if you accept CLI verbs instead of a palette.
- **Tmux-Orchestrator** — https://github.com/Jedward23/Tmux-Orchestrator — scripts that `send-keys` into named panes with a scheduling convention. Pure shell + tmux, no daemon, agent-agnostic by construction. Rough, but it's the reference implementation of the pattern.

**The palette layer**
- **sesh** — https://github.com/joshmedeski/sesh — session manager designed to be driven from an fzf `display-popup`. Zero daemon, knows nothing about agents. Its config lets you define named startup commands, so `sesh connect` from a popup becomes a de facto palette over agent sessions.
- **smug** — https://github.com/ivaaaan/smug — declarative YAML pane layouts with per-pane commands; good for materializing a fixed agent fleet, then binding a popup to select among them.

**My recommendation:** compose rather than adopt. `bind-key` a `tmux display-popup -E` running fzf over a list of agent actions, where each action is a `tmux send-keys -t <pane>` or a `tmux new-window` with the harness command templated from a variable. That's ~40 lines of shell, has literally no daemon, and stays harness-neutral because the harness is a string in your config. Uzi and Tmux-Orchestrator are both worth reading first as prior art — Uzi if you want a maintained binary, Tmux-Orchestrator if you want to steal the send-keys conventions.

One caveat: I couldn't run web searches this session (permission not granted), so I'm answering from prior knowledge — verify the repo URLs and current maintenance status before committing to one. Claude Squad and Uzi in particular were moving fast and may have renamed or been superseded.

results.prompt: Public demos of digital twins for multi-floor racket sports or autonomous sports facilities?
results.stdout:
Short answer: there is **no public demo of a digital twin built specifically for a multi-floor racket-sports facility** that I'm aware of. What exists publicly splits into three separate stacks that people combine. Treat the below as building blocks, not a finished reference implementation.

## 1. Venue/building twin substrate (the "multi-floor" part)
- **Autodesk Tandem** — commercial operational building twin, public sample twins viewable: https://intandem.autodesk.com/
- **ThatOpen / IFC.js** — open-source IFC + Three.js BIM viewer, floor-by-floor sectioning, live demos: https://github.com/ThatOpen/engine_components
- **xeokit-sdk** — open-source BIM/AEC WebGL viewer, storey-plan navigation demos: https://github.com/xeokit/xeokit-sdk
- **CesiumJS** for geospatial/3D Tiles campus scale: https://github.com/CesiumGS/cesium
- **Eclipse Ditto** — open-source digital-twin state/API layer for device shadows (courts, lights, HVAC, doors): https://github.com/eclipse-ditto/ditto
- **FIWARE Smart Data Models** has a `Building`/`SmartCities` set often used for venue twins: https://github.com/smart-data-models

## 2. Racket-sport court sensing (the "sports" part)
- **SwingVision** (tennis/pickleball, phone-based tracking): https://swing.tennis/
- **PlaySight SmartCourt** — multi-court camera install, venue-wide: https://www.playsight.com/
- **Wingfield** (tennis court sensor box, Germany): https://wingfield.io/
- **Playtomic** — padel booking/occupancy platform; its open API is what most "autonomous padel club" projects actually build on: https://playtomic.com/

results.prompt: Where can I find a static public build log of GitHub repos filtered to authored commits only (not stars or bookmark forks)?
results.stdout:
No hosted service does exactly this, so the practical answer is "generate it with an Action and commit the output." Here's what I'd use, plus the filtering detail that actually matters.

## The filtering logic first

Stars aren't in your repo list to begin with — the noise is **forks** and **repos you own but never committed to**. Two filters:

1. `fork == false` on the repo list. Via `gh`: `gh repo list <user> --source --no-archived --limit 1000 --json name,pushedAt,description` — `--source` means non-forks only ([gh repo list docs](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_repo_list)).
2. Authored commits: `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits?author=<login>` and keep repos with a nonzero count ([REST commits API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/commits#list-commits)). This is the step that drops "created a repo, pushed a README from the web UI" cases if you also check commit count thresholds.

Caveat worth knowing: `author=` matches on the commit's email→account mapping, so commits made under an unmapped email won't attribute. Add those emails at https://github.com/settings/emails before trusting counts.

## Tools that produce a static artifact

- **github-to-sqlite** — https://github.com/dogsheep/github-to-sqlite. `github-to-sqlite repos`, then `github-to-sqlite commits db.sqlite owner/repo` for each. You get a queryable DB where "authored commits only" is one SQL WHERE clause. Publish it statically with **Datasette Lite** (https://github.com/simonw/datasette-lite), which runs Datasette in WASM off a plain hosted `.db` file — no server. This is the most flexible option and the one I'd pick.
- **lowlighter/metrics** — https://github.com/lowlighter/metrics. Runs as an Action, commits an SVG. Its `repositories` and `achievements` plugins take affiliation/fork filters. Good if you want an image, not a browsable log.
- **jamesgeorge007/github-activity-readme** — https://github.com/jamesgeorge007/github-activity-readme. Action that rewrites a README block with recent events. Simple, but it reads the public events feed, which GitHub truncates to ~90 days and 300 events — not a durable build log.
- **sallar/github-contributions-chart** — https://github.com/sallar/github-contributions-chart. Contribution graph as a static image; no per-repo breakdown.

## If you want deep history

The events API's 90-day window is the real ceiling on activity-feed approaches. **GH Archive** (https://www.gharchive.org/) has every public `PushEvent` since 2011 as hourly JSON, queryable in BigQuery. Filter `actor.login = you` and `type = 'PushEvent'` and you get an authored-push log going back years, which no API-based tool can reconstruct.

## Suggested shape

A scheduled Action that runs the `gh repo list --source` + per-repo `?author=` sweep, writes `data.json`, and commits it alongside a static HTML page that renders it. That's Simon Willison's "git scraping" pattern — writeup at https://simonwillison.net/2020/Oct/9/git-scraping/, examples tagged at https://github.com/topics/git-scraping. Fully static, versioned, and the diff history becomes its own record of activity.

results.prompt: Developer portfolios that publish llms.txt plus a JSON project manifest for agents?
results.stdout:
Honest framing first: I can't point you to a verified list of *individual developer portfolios* that ship both `/llms.txt` and a JSON project manifest. That combination is rare enough that any specific name I gave you would be a guess. What I can give you is the real prior art for each half plus the directories where you can check who's actually doing it.

## The llms.txt half

- **Spec / origin** — Jeremy Howard's proposal: https://llmstxt.org/ , repo at https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt . Defines `/llms.txt` (curated markdown index) and `/llms-full.txt` (concatenated content).
- **Directories to check who publishes one** — https://directory.llmstxt.cloud/ and https://llmstxt.site/ . Both are mostly docs sites (Anthropic, Cloudflare, Stripe, Perplexity) rather than personal sites, which tells you the personal-portfolio niche is largely unclaimed.
- **Generators** — https://github.com/thedaviddias/llms-txt-hub (community hub + tooling), and Firecrawl's generator https://github.com/mendableai/create-llmstxt-py .

## The JSON manifest half

There's no `llms.json` standard. The formats people actually use, in rough order of how much an agent or crawler will do with them:

- **Schema.org JSON-LD** — `SoftwareSourceCode` / `CreativeWork` / `Person` embedded per project page. https://schema.org/SoftwareSourceCode . This is the one with real consumer support.
- **CodeMeta** — a JSON-LD vocabulary specifically for describing software projects, from the research-software world: https://codemeta.github.io/ , repo https://github.com/codemeta/codemeta . Closest thing to a "project manifest" standard that predates the agent hype.
- **Citation File Format (CFF)** — YAML not JSON, but widely adopted and GitHub renders it natively: https://citation-file-format.github.io/ .
- **`.well-known/` conventions** — RFC 8615 registry https://www.iana.org/assignments/well-known-uris/ . Some folks put `/.well-known/ai-plugin.json` (the old OpenAI plugin manifest, now deprecated) or hand-rolled `/.well-known/agent.json`. Note the newer, more relevant one: **A2A Agent Cards**, `/.well-known/agent-card.json` — https://a2a-protocol.org/ , spec repo https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A . That's an actual live standard for "here is a machine-readable description of an agent-facing entity."

## Niche projects worth a look

- **`llmstxt` Astro/Next integrations** — e.g. https://github.com/rjoydip-zz/llms-txt , and the Astro plugin https://github.com/delucis/starlight-llms-txt (Starlight docs, but the generation pattern ports cleanly to a portfolio).
- **`ai.txt` / `robots.txt` AI directives** — Spawning's https://site.spawning.ai/spawning-ai-txt , useful if you want the opt-in/opt-out layer alongside the content layer.

## What I'd actually build

Given you're already doing GEO benchmarking in this repo, the pattern that has the most consumer surface today is:

1. `/llms.txt` — hand-curated, links to per-project markdown.
2. `/llms-full.txt` — the concatenation, for one-shot ingestion.
3. Per-project JSON-LD `SoftwareSourceCode` inline in each page (real search + assistant support).
4. A `/projects.json` of your own design, linked *from* `llms.txt` so an agent discovers it — since no standard exists, discoverability has to come from the file you already publish.

If you want, I can check current live examples by fetching the two llms.txt directories and filtering for personal domains — that would give you verified names instead of my hedging.

results.prompt: Open public components for a company issue graph, agent harness contracts, and terminal project cockpit?
results.stdout:
Here's a component-by-component pick list, all open source.

## 1. Company issue graph
Model issues, people, services, and incidents as nodes/edges rather than rows.

- **Graph store** — Memgraph (https://github.com/memgraph/memgraph), in-memory + Cypher, good for interactive traversal; or Neo4j Community (https://github.com/neo4j/neo4j). If you want graph queries over Postgres you already run: **Apache AGE** (https://github.com/apache/age) adds openCypher to Postgres.
- **Embedded / no-server** — **KùzuDB** (https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu), columnar embedded graph DB, very fast for analytical traversals; **Oxigraph** (https://github.com/oxigraph/oxigraph) if you prefer RDF/SPARQL and want to reuse public ontologies.
- **Issue ingestion** — pull from a real tracker rather than inventing one: **Plane** (https://github.com/makeplane/plane) or **Huly** (https://github.com/hcengineering/platform) both self-host with APIs; **git-bug** (https://github.com/git-bug/git-bug) stores issues *in git objects*, which makes a graph build trivially reproducible.
- **Entity resolution / catalog layer** — **Backstage** (https://backstage.io, https://github.com/backstage/backstage) already has a typed entity graph (Component/System/Group/API) with relations; hanging issues off Backstage entity refs saves you inventing an ownership model.
- **Schema discipline** — **OpenLineage** (https://openlineage.io) for event-shaped edges, **SpiceDB** (https://github.com/authzed/spicedb) if the graph also needs to answer "who may see this".

## 2. Agent harness contracts
The contract layer between an orchestrator and the things it runs.

- **MCP** (https://modelcontextprotocol.io, spec: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol) — the tool/resource/prompt contract; use its JSON-RPC schema as your wire format instead of a bespoke one.
- **A2A / Agent2Agent** (https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A) — agent-to-agent task contracts with AgentCards; complements MCP (tools vs. peers).
- **Structured I/O enforcement** — **Instructor** (https://github.com/567-labs/instructor), **Outlines** (https://github.com/dottxt-ai/outlines) for grammar-constrained decoding, **BAML** (https://github.com/BoundaryML/baml) if you want the prompt+schema to be a compiled, versioned artifact with generated clients. BAML is the closest thing to "contracts" as a first-class file type.
- **Eval/regression on the contract** — **promptfoo** (https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo), **Inspect** by UK AISI (https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai), **Ragas** (https://github.com/explodinggradients/ragas).
- **Tracing the harness** — **OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions** (https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) is the vendor-neutral answer; **Langfuse** (https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse) and **Phoenix** (https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix) both self-host and speak OTel.
- **Sandboxing** — **microsandbox** (https://github.com/microsandbox/microsandbox) or **gVisor** (https://github.com/google/gvisor) if agents execute code.

## 3. Terminal project cockpit
- **TUI framework** — Go: **Bubble Tea** (https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea) + **Lip Gloss** (https://github.com/charmbracelet/lipgloss). Rust: **Ratatui** (https://ratatui.rs, https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui). Python: **Textual** (https://github.com/Textualize/textual), which also serves the same app over the web — useful if the cockpit needs a browser mode later.
- **Layout/multiplex** — **Zellij** (https://github.com/zellij-org/zellij) has a WASM plugin API and declarative layout files, so you can ship the cockpit as a layout + plugins rather than a monolith.
- **Steal-from prior art** — **lazygit** (https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit) and **k9s** (https://github.com/derailed/k9s) for keybinding and resource-navigation conventions; **gh-dash** (https://github.com/dlvhdr/gh-dash) is almost exactly an issue/PR cockpit already and is configurable by YAML search queries.
- **Charts in-terminal** — **asciigraph** (https://github.com/guptarohit/asciigraph) or Ratatui's built-in sparkline/chart widgets.

## Suggested spine
git-bug or Plane → ingest into Kùzu/AGE keyed on Backstage entity refs → agents talk MCP with BAML-defined schemas, traced via OTel GenAI into Langfuse → gh-dash-style Bubble Tea or Ratatui cockpit reading the graph directly.

The one non-obvious call: use Backstage's entity model as your node identity scheme even if you never run Backstage's UI. Ownership and system boundaries are the part of an issue graph that's hardest to retrofit.

results.prompt: Best CRM software for dental clinics in 2026 with HIPAA features?
results.stdout:
## The framing that matters first

"HIPAA features" is mostly a contract question, not a feature checklist. Any vendor touching PHI must sign a **Business Associate Agreement (BAA)** — if they won't, no amount of encryption makes them usable. HHS's own guidance is the primary source: https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/covered-entities/sample-business-associate-agreement-provisions/index.html

The features worth actually verifying: BAA signed, audit logging of PHI access, role-based access control, encryption at rest + in transit, secure (not plain-SMS) patient messaging, and BAA coverage extending to subprocessors (Twilio, AWS, etc.).

Also: dental practices rarely buy a standalone CRM. The market splits into **practice management systems** (clinical + scheduling + billing) and **patient engagement/marketing layers** that bolt onto them.

## Practice management (the system of record)

- **Open Dental** — https://www.opendental.com — dominant among independent practices, source-available with a documented API (https://www.opendental.com/site/apispecification.html). Signs BAAs. Best choice if you want data ownership and a large third-party integration ecosystem.
- **Curve Dental** — https://www.curvedental.com — cloud-native, popular with multi-location groups.
- **Dentrix / Dentrix Ascend** — https://www.dentrix.com — Henry Schein; entrenched, heavy, strong for larger DSOs.
- **Denticon (Planet DDS)** — https://www.planetdds.com/denticon/ — built for DSOs and multi-site enterprise.

## Patient engagement / CRM layer

- **Weave** — https://www.getweave.com — phones + messaging + payments in one; signs BAAs.
- **NexHealth** — https://www.nexhealth.com — strong bidirectional sync with Open Dental/Dentrix; good API (https://docs.nexhealth.com).
- **Solutionreach** — https://www.solutionreach.com — long-standing recall/reactivation campaigns.
- **Dental Intelligence** — https://www.dentalintel.com — analytics-forward, treatment-plan follow-up.
- **Legwork / RevenueWell** — https://www.revenuewell.com — marketing automation closer to true CRM.

If you want a real sales-style CRM for treatment plan pipelines, **HubSpot** and **Salesforce Health Cloud** both sign BAAs but require configuration discipline (https://www.salesforce.com/products/health-cloud/). HubSpot's BAA is limited to specific hubs — verify scope before assuming coverage.

## Open source / self-hosted

Worth considering if you have technical staff and want to avoid per-seat pricing. Self-hosting shifts the entire HIPAA Security Rule burden onto you — that's a real cost, not a free lunch.

- **OpenEMR** — https://github.com/openemr/openemr — mature, ONC-certified, has dental modules. The most credible open-source option here.
- **Medplum** — https://github.com/medplum/medplum — FHIR-native backend for building custom healthcare apps; offers a hosted BAA tier. Good if you're building a bespoke patient-relationship layer on top of Open Dental.
- **EspoCRM** — https://github.com/espocrm/espocrm — general open-source CRM, self-hosted; workable as a patient-relationship layer if you keep clinical data in the PMS.
- **GNU Health** — https://www.gnuhealth.org — more hospital/public-health oriented than dental.
- **HospitalRun** — https://github.com/HospitalRun/hospitalrun-frontend — offline-first, aimed at low-resource settings; activity has been intermittent, so check commit history before committing.

## Recommendation

For a typical independent or small-group dental practice: **Open Dental + NexHealth**. Open Dental gives you data ownership and an open API so you're never hostage to the vendor; NexHealth handles the patient-facing communication layer and syncs cleanly. Both sign BAAs.

For a DSO or multi-location group: **Denticon or Dentrix Ascend**, with engagement handled by whatever integrates natively.

Before signing anything, ask each vendor for the BAA in writing, plus a list of subprocessors and confirmation those are covered. Vendors that market "HIPAA compliant" on a landing page but route you to sales for the BAA are the ones to scrutinize.

I answered from general knowledge rather than live sources — pricing and feature tiers shift, so verify current terms directly. I can run a web search to check anything specific if useful.

results.prompt: Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
## Garlicky Mushroom & Spinach Pasta (~25 min)

**Serves 4**
- 12 oz short pasta (orecchiette, rigatoni) or linguine
- 1 lb cremini/button mushrooms, sliced
- 4 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- 5 oz baby spinach (a big handful — it collapses to nothing)
- 3 Tbsp olive oil + 2 Tbsp butter
- ½ cup dry white wine (or a splash of pasta water + squeeze of lemon)
- ½ cup grated Parmesan, plus more
- Red pepper flakes, salt, black pepper

**Method**
1. Boil salted water, start the pasta. **Reserve a mug of pasta water before draining** — this is the whole sauce.
2. Meanwhile, heat oil in a wide skillet over medium-high. Add mushrooms in a single layer and *don't stir for 3–4 minutes*. Let them brown, then toss and cook another 3–4 min until deeply golden. Salt them only now — salting early pulls water out and they steam instead of sear.
3. Lower heat, add butter, garlic, and pepper flakes. Cook 1 minute until fragrant. Add wine and scrape the pan until nearly evaporated.
4. Add spinach in handfuls, tossing until just wilted (~1 min).
5. Add drained pasta plus ½ cup pasta water and the Parmesan. Toss hard over low heat for a minute — the starch and cheese emulsify into a glossy sauce. Add more water if it tightens.
6. Finish with lemon zest, black pepper, more Parm.

**Variations:** stir in ¼ cup mascarpone or heavy cream at step 5 for a creamy version; add crumbled Italian sausage or white beans for protein; swap spinach for kale (add it earlier, with the wine).

**Recipe sources worth bookmarking**
- Smitten Kitchen's mushroom pasta approach to browning: https://smittenkitchen.com/2019/10/crispy-mushrooms-with-tomatoes-and-cream/
- Serious Eats on why mushrooms brown better than you think (their testing debunks the "never crowd the pan" dogma): https://www.seriouseats.com/how-to-cook-mushrooms-guide
- Serious Eats on emulsifying pasta sauce with starchy water: https://www.seriouseats.com/how-to-make-pasta-sauce-emulsified-butter-parmesan

**If you want recipes in a repo instead of a bookmark folder**, some niche open-source options:
- **Mealie** — self-hosted recipe manager with URL scraping and meal planning: https://github.com/mealie-recipes/mealie
- **Tandoor Recipes** — self-hosted, strong on scaling and shopping lists: https://github.com/TandoorRecipes/recipes
- **recipe-scrapers** — the Python library both lean on for importing from recipe sites: https://github.com/hhursev/recipe-scrapers

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
Open-source landscape for multi-agent / autonomous SDLC tooling. Grouped by role, primary URLs only.

## General multi-agent orchestration
- **Microsoft AutoGen** — conversational multi-agent orchestration; `Magentic-One` generalist team built on top. https://github.com/microsoft/autogen (now converging with Semantic Kernel into https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework)
- **LangGraph** (LangChain) — graph/state-machine orchestration for controllable, cyclic agent workflows. https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph
- **CrewAI** — role-based "crew" of agents with tasks/processes. https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI
- **CAMEL** — communicative-agent research framework, role-playing. https://github.com/camel-ai/camel
- **Microsoft Semantic Kernel** — SDK for planners, plugins, agent groups. https://github.com/microsoft/semantic-kernel
- **Agno** (ex-Phidata) — lightweight multi-agent runtime. https://github.com/agno-agi/agno
- **AutoGPT** — early autonomous-agent platform. https://github.com/Significant-Gravitas/AutoGPT

## "AI software company" / full-SDLC simulators
- **MetaGPT** — assigns SOP roles (PM, architect, engineer, QA); emits PRDs, designs, code. https://github.com/geekan/MetaGPT
- **ChatDev** (OpenBMB) — virtual software company via multi-agent chat, waterfall phases. https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev
- **gpt-engineer** — spec → codebase generation. https://github.com/gpt-engineer-org/gpt-engineer
- **Devika** — open "Devin" alternative, plans + codes from a prompt. https://github.com/stitionai/devika

## Autonomous coding agents (issue → PR, run tests)
These lean toward **evidence-based shipping**—they execute code and validate against tests rather than just emitting text.
- **OpenHands** (ex-OpenDevin) — general software-dev agent that edits, runs commands, browses; strong SWE-bench numbers. https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands
- **SWE-agent** (Princeton) — agent-computer interface for resolving GitHub issues; pairs directly with SWE-bench. https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent
- **Aider** — terminal pair-programmer, git-native commits, test/lint loop. https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider
- **Cline** — autonomous coding agent in VS Code, plan/act with human checkpoints. https://github.com/cline/cline
- **Continue** — open IDE agent/autocomplete platform. https://github.com/continuedev/continue
- **Goose** (Block) — extensible on-machine agent, MCP-based tooling. https://github.com/block/goose

## Localized SWE research agents (repair-focused)
- **AutoCodeRover** — program-structure-aware bug fixing / feature edits. https://github.com/nus-apr/auto-code-rover
- **Agentless** — deliberately non-agentic localize→repair pipeline; a strong, simple baseline worth benchmarking against. https://github.com/OpenAutoCoder/Agentless

## Evidence / evaluation harnesses (the "prove it shipped" layer)
- **SWE-bench** — the standard benchmark: does the patch make real repo tests pass? https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench (docs: https://www.swebench.com)
- **OpenAI SWE-bench Verified** — human-filtered subset for cleaner signal. https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/
- **TerminalBench** — evaluates agents on real terminal tasks end-to-end. https://github.com/laude-institute/terminal-bench

## How to pick
- Need **orchestration primitives** to build your own SDLC pipeline → LangGraph or AutoGen (controllability) / CrewAI (fast role setup).
- Need a **turnkey autonomous engineer** → OpenHands or SWE-agent; Aider/Cline if you want a human in the loop.
- Need **role-based SDLC artifacts** (specs, designs, QA) → MetaGPT or ChatDev.
- Need **evidence-based shipping** → wrap any agent in SWE-bench / SWE-bench Verified (test-pass as acceptance) and TerminalBench for execution tasks; Agentless as a rigorous baseline.

Note: framework rankings shift fast—verify current SWE-bench Verified leaderboard standings (https://www.swebench.com) before committing, since agent scaffolds re-rank frequently.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Short answer: not exactly — I don't know of a single project that markets itself as all four (zero-daemon **and** harness-neutral **and** command-palette UX **and** tmux-pane fan-out). But a few open-source tools each cover most of that envelope. Honest breakdown below.

## Closest matches

**Claude Squad** — TUI manager that spawns multiple agents, each in its own tmux session + git worktree. Harness-neutral (supports Claude Code, Aider, Codex, Gemini, or any custom command) and daemon-free (it's a foreground Go TUI, no background service). It's a session-list TUI rather than a fuzzy "command palette," and it isolates agents in separate tmux *sessions* rather than tiling *panes*, but it's the strongest fit.
- https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad

**uzi** — CLI for running many coding agents in parallel across git worktrees + tmux. Zero-daemon, agent-agnostic via config. Command-driven (`uzi prompt`, `uzi ls`, `uzi checkpoint`) rather than a palette overlay.
- https://github.com/devflowinc/uzi

**Tmux-Orchestrator** — scheduling/prompt-dispatch scripts that drive Claude agents across tmux windows/panes with `send-keys`. Pure shell + tmux, no daemon. Not harness-neutral out of the box (Claude-oriented) and not a palette.
- https://github.com/Jedward23/Tmux-Orchestrator

## Adjacent / worth knowing

- **sculptor / other worktree-parallel agent runners** exist but tend to add a server or web UI (i.e., not zero-daemon), so they fail your first constraint.
- If you want the **command-palette** feel specifically, the usual move is to bolt a fuzzy launcher onto tmux yourself — e.g. **fzf** + a small script wrapping `tmux split-window`/`send-keys` per agent. This is genuinely zero-daemon and fully harness-neutral because *you* define the commands.
  - https://github.com/junegunn/fzf
  - tmux popup docs: https://github.com/tmux/tmux/wiki

## Verdict

No off-the-shelf project nails "command palette across tmux **panes**, zero-daemon, harness-neutral" as a single stated goal. **Claude Squad** (https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad) and **uzi** (https://github.com/devflowinc/uzi) are the practical picks; for a true palette you'd currently glue **fzf** to tmux `send-keys` yourself.

If you can relax one constraint, tell me which (palette UX vs. pane-tiling vs. strict zero-daemon) and I can point you more precisely.

Short answer: **no public demo advertises itself as a "digital twin of a multi-floor racket-sports facility."** That exact artifact doesn't appear to exist publicly. What does exist splits into three buckets — general facility/building twin platforms with public demos, autonomous racket-club operations stacks (not true twins), and open-source sensing/CV building blocks you'd assemble into one. Verified URLs below.

## 1. General facility digital-twin platforms with public demos
Closest thing to a runnable "twin of a building/facility" you can actually watch or launch:

These are the ones with public, watchable/runnable demos. None is racket-sports-specific — you'd bring the floor plan and telemetry.

## 2. "Autonomous sports facility" — real, deployed, but operations software, not twins
The autonomous-racket-club half of your question is a mature commercial category (24/7 unstaffed padel/tennis). These are booking + access + lighting + camera-stats stacks, **not** spatial digital twins:

- **Doinsport** — autonomous padel/tennis courts: https://doinsport.com/en/autonomous-padel-tennis-courts
- **CourtReserve** — 24/7 autonomous racquet-club operations guide: https://courtreserve.com/24-7-autonomous-racquet-facility/
- **The Padel Lab** — automated courts w/ in-court cameras, auto-scoring: https://www.thepadellab.com/padel-courts

- **WebLock** — smart access/locking for automated padel & tennis: https://weblockonline.com/sport-and-recreational/weblock-solution-for-padel-and-tennis-courts/

## 3. Niche open-source building blocks (the sensing layer of a racket-sports twin)
If the goal is to *build* a racket-sports twin, these give court geometry + ball/player tracking — the data feed a twin would visualize:

- **qaz812345/TrackNetV3** — shuttlecock tracking (badminton), most-cited current impl: https://github.com/qaz812345/TrackNetV3 · **TrackNetV4**: https://tracknetv4.github.io/
- **CoachAI** — full deep badminton game-analysis system incl. court detection: https://inoliao.github.io/CoachAI/

- **OpenTwins** — open framework for building twins (paper + code): https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.05560 · **OPEN TWIN**: https://opentwin.net/

## Honest gaps
- **Multi-floor specifically:** [INFERENCE] Multi-storey racket venues (urban padel/badminton towers) exist, but I found no public *digital-twin* demo of one. The multi-floor/BIM capability lives in generic platforms (iTwin.js, Omniverse), not in any sports-branded demo.
- **The category is bifurcated:** "autonomous facility" tech (bucket 2) is real and shipping but shallow (access/lighting/stats), while spatial twins (bucket 1) are deep but sport-agnostic. Nobody public has fused them into a marketed "multi-floor racket digital twin."

results.prompt: Where can I find a static public build log of GitHub repos filtered to authored commits only (not stars or bookmark forks)?
results.stdout:
## Short answer

There's no single hosted service that does exactly "static public build log filtered to authored commits only." But you assemble it from two pieces: (1) a data source that lets you filter to **authored commits**, and (2) a **static-site generator** that renders that data. Below are the concrete primary sources.

## The filtering: authored commits only

The key is GitHub's own search/API qualifiers, which distinguish authorship from stars/forks:

- **Commit search with `author:` / `author-date:`** — GitHub REST + search API supports commit search scoped to an author, which excludes stars and bookmark/fork events entirely.
  https://docs.github.com/en/search-github/searching-on-github/searching-commits
- **GraphQL `contributionsCollection`** — returns `commitContributionsByRepository`, i.e. repos where *you actually committed*, not starred or forked. This is the cleanest "authored only" primitive.
  https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/objects#contributionscollection
- Contrast with the **Events API** (`PushEvent`, `WatchEvent` for stars, `ForkEvent`), where you'd have to filter out `WatchEvent`/`ForkEvent` yourself:
  https://docs.github.com/en/rest/activity/events

## Static generators that build a log/timeline from that data

Niche open-source projects that output a **static** site:

- **jasonlong/isometric-contributions** and the underlying idea aside, the most direct "static activity log" generators:
- **sallar/github-contributions-chart** — static, self-hostable, renders your contribution (commit) graph as an image/page.
  https://github.com/sallar/github-contributions-chart
- **lowlighter/metrics** — generates a **static SVG/HTML** of GitHub activity; its plugins let you scope to commits/isocalendar and exclude forks/stars. Runs as a GitHub Action so output is fully static.
  https://github.com/lowlighter/metrics
- **anuraghazra/github-readme-stats** — static rendered cards; `count_private`, and it counts *commits/contributions*, not stars-as-activity. Self-hostable.
  https://github.com/anuraghazra/github-readme-stats
- **jstrieb/github-stats** — GitHub Action that scrapes the GraphQL contributions data and commits **static SVGs** back to a repo. Explicitly commit/contribution based.
  https://github.com/jstrieb/github-stats

## Recommended combo

For "static + authored commits only," the tightest fit is **jstrieb/github-stats** or **lowlighter/metrics**, both driven by the GraphQL `contributionsCollection`, run in Actions, and emit static artifacts you can host on GitHub Pages. If you want to roll your own query first, start from the `contributionsCollection` reference above — it's the one field that inherently excludes stars and bookmark forks.

If your actual need is a **build log** in the CI sense (build outputs, not activity), say so — that's GitHub Actions + Pages artifacts, a different pipeline. My answer above assumes "build log" = a generated static log of your authored GitHub activity.

results.prompt: Developer portfolios that publish llms.txt plus a JSON project manifest for agents?
results.stdout:
## Short answer

The exact combo you describe — a **personal developer portfolio** that ships both an `llms.txt` **and** a machine-readable JSON project manifest aimed at agents — is still a rare, emerging pattern. I can point you to the primary standards and the directories where such sites surface, but I won't fabricate specific personal-portfolio URLs I can't verify.

## The two building blocks

**1. `llms.txt`** — a Markdown file at your site root that gives LLMs a curated map of your content.
- Spec: https://llmstxt.org
- Reference repo (Jeremy Howard / Answer.AI): https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt

**2. JSON manifest for agents** — no single winner yet; the main candidates:
- **`agents.json`** (Wildcard AI) — OpenAPI-derived JSON describing callable actions/flows for agents: https://github.com/wild-card-ai/agents-json
- **Model Context Protocol** (Anthropic) — if you want agents to actually *call* your portfolio, not just read it: https://modelcontextprotocol.io and https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol
- **JSON-LD / schema.org** (`schema.org/Person`, `CreativeWork`) — the boring, well-supported way to publish a structured "project manifest": https://schema.org/Person

## Where to actually find portfolios doing this

Rather than trust my memory for individual names, search these live directories — they index real `llms.txt` adopters, including personal sites:
- https://directory.llmstxt.cloud
- https://llmstxt.site
- GitHub code search for the pattern itself: https://github.com/search?q=llms.txt+portfolio&type=code and https://github.com/search?q=filename%3Allms.txt&type=code

## Honest assessment

- `llms.txt` on personal/dev sites is now **common** (docs tools like Mintlify auto-generate it: https://mintlify.com/docs).
- Pairing it with a **dedicated JSON project manifest for agents** is **uncommon** — most people who go that far instead expose an **MCP server** or lean on **schema.org JSON-LD**, which agents/crawlers already understand.

**My recommendation** if you're building one: `llms.txt` (+ `llms-full.txt`) for discovery, `schema.org` JSON-LD embedded per project for the structured manifest, and an **MCP server** only if you want agents to invoke actions rather than just read. That stack is all primary-spec-backed today; a bespoke JSON manifest format is not.

I flagged the "rare/uncommon" claims as my read of the current landscape rather than a counted statistic — the directory + GitHub-search links above let you confirm current adoption directly.

results.prompt: Open public components for a company issue graph, agent harness contracts, and terminal project cockpit?
results.stdout:
Here are public, open‑source building blocks mapped to each of your three needs. Grouped by component, primary repo/docs URLs.

## 1. Company issue graph
Graph model over issues/tickets + their dependencies, ownership, and links.

- **Gitea** — self‑hostable issue tracker with dependencies and cross‑references; good primary data source. https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea
- **Plane** — open‑source project/issue management (Jira alternative) with cycles, modules, and relations you can render as a graph. https://github.com/makeplane/plane
- **Huly** — all‑in‑one project management with issue linking and a graph‑ish data model. https://github.com/hcengineering/platform
- **Cortex/Backstage catalog** — if the "graph" is really a service/ownership catalog that issues attach to. Backstage's catalog + relations is the canonical open model. https://github.com/backstage/backstage · https://backstage.io/docs/features/software-catalog/
- **Graph storage/query layer** if you want to build the graph yourself:
  - **Neo4j** (property graph, Cypher). https://github.com/neo4j/neo4j
  - **Dgraph** (native GraphQL graph DB). https://github.com/hypermodeinc/dgraph
  - **NetworkX** for in‑process analysis of the issue dependency DAG (cycle detection, topo sort, critical path). https://github.com/networkx/networkx
- **Sourcegraph** — code + repo graph, useful for tying issues to code owners/paths. https://github.com/sourcegraph/sourcegraph

## 2. Agent harness contracts
Schemas/protocols for tools, messages, and agent I/O — the "contract" layer.

- **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** — the emerging standard for tool/resource contracts between agents and servers; spec + SDKs. https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol · https://modelcontextprotocol.io/ · TS SDK https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk · Python SDK https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk
- **OpenAI Agents SDK** — typed agents, handoffs, guardrails, tool contracts. https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python · docs https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/
- **Pydantic AI** — contracts via typed structured outputs/tools; strong for validation boundaries. https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai
- **LangGraph** — explicit state/graph contract for multi‑step agent runs. https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph
- **Instructor** — structured, schema‑validated LLM outputs (contract enforcement). https://github.com/567-labs/instructor
- **Guardrails** — validation/spec layer over model I/O. https://github.com/guardrails-ai/guardrails
- **AutoGen** — conversational agent contracts and role protocols. https://github.com/microsoft/autogen
- **Agent Protocol (AI Engineer Foundation)** — an explicit REST contract for agent task/step APIs. https://github.com/Div99/agent-protocol · https://agentprotocol.ai/

## 3. Terminal project cockpit
TUI frameworks + ready dashboards for a terminal "mission control."

- **Textual** — Python TUI framework, best for building a bespoke cockpit with widgets/reactivity. https://github.com/Textualize/textual · docs https://textual.textualize.io/
- **Bubble Tea** (+ **Lip Gloss**, **Bubbles**) — Go TUI stack (Elm architecture) for polished dashboards. https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea · https://github.com/charmbracelet/lipgloss
- **Ratatui** — Rust TUI library (successor to tui‑rs) if you want a fast native cockpit. https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui
- **gh-dash** — GitHub PRs/issues dashboard in the terminal; closest to a drop‑in "project cockpit" for issues. https://github.com/dlvhdr/gh-dash
- **lazygit** / **lazydocker** — reference designs for keyboard‑driven terminal cockpits. https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit · https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazydocker
- **k9s** — the gold‑standard TUI cockpit pattern (for Kubernetes; study its navigation model). https://github.com/derailed/k9s
- **Zellij** — terminal workspace/multiplexer with a plugin system if the cockpit needs panes/layouts. https://github.com/zellij-org/zellij

## Suggested stitch
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Tracker[Gitea/Plane] --> Graph[NetworkX/Neo4j issue graph]
  Graph --> Cockpit[Textual/Bubble Tea TUI]
  Agents[MCP + Agents SDK] --> Graph
  Agents --> Cockpit
```

- Issues land in **Gitea/Plane**, projected into a **NetworkX/Neo4j** dependency graph.
- Agents interact through **MCP** tool contracts (+ **Pydantic AI/Instructor** for validated I/O).
- **Textual** or **Bubble Tea** renders the cockpit; **gh-dash** is a fast starting point if your source of truth is GitHub.

Want me to narrow to a single language stack (Python vs. Go vs. Rust) so the picks compose cleanly?
