...
The 244-inch diagonal Radiance Performance Series 1.2mm COB, (Chip-On-Board) LED video wall from Digital Projection** **occupies a custom, high-end theater.** **Designed, integrated, and commissioned by Invictus, the video wall featured in the “Invictus Sports Theater” creates the ultimate sports-viewing venue.
...
The theater, which seats 43 guests at tables, functions as an upscale private viewing room where patrons can reserve seats during special events like March Madness or NFL Sundays. Complementing the visuals is a Dolby Atmos audio system featuring Sonance Reference Series in-wall and in-ceiling speakers and Origin Acoustics audio amplifiers. On command from a specially programmed remote from Universal Remote Control, an AV Pro Edge MXNet video matrix feeds content from a centralized rack of AV equipment to the video wall and all other displays in the Bosse Pickledom.
...
From the very beginning of the Bosse Pickledom project, the Digital Projection Radiance LED video wall was envisioned as the crown jewel of a $2 million AV strategy—and marked Invictus’ maiden voyage into the world of LED video wall integration. “Certainly, our team could have managed the installation ourselves,” Bettencourt said, “but for a project of this scale and visibility, Digital Projection’s white glove service was the smarter path. Their expert technicians completed the installation in just a few days, allowing our team to concentrate on the many other layers of the project, including distributed audio for 21 pickleball courts, extensive Wi-Fi coverage, and a comprehensive surveillance and access control system.”
...
Guided by the client’s vision, Digital Projection technicians collaborated closely with the Invictus team to seamlessly integrate the massive video wall within the architectural constraints of the theater. A projector-based solution was quickly ruled out due to high ambient light levels, limited ceiling height, and the client’s specific aesthetic and performance preferences.
...
After carefully assessing the space, the team settled on an 18x10-foot, 244-inch diagonal video wall, comprised of roughly 81 panels and 650 individual 6x6.5-inch LED modules delivered direct from Digital Projection to the jobsite in pre-labeled road cases. Each module was clearly numbered and mapped to its exact placement on a custom metal framing structure. While the Digital Projection tech team configured the massive display, Invictus created a cavity into which the video wall would be recessed to create a flush, seamless appearance.
...
“It was a nice surprise to learn that Digital Projection would supply spare LED modules to use later if we ever need them,” remarks Bettencourt. “As is Digital Projection’s standard practice, these were pulled from the same manufacturing bin and batch as the originals to ensure color consistency during any future replacements.” Even the theater’s AV system offers flexibility: while it’s optimized for one massive picture, a multi-view card allows the wall to split into four separate feeds, raising the ever-present question of which audio feed to prioritize—a challenge Invictus is happy to tackle as the venue continues to evolve.
...
The theater wasn't the only upgrade. With 50,000 square feet on each level, the Bosse Pickledom is massive. The upper floor features several restaurants, including a full-scale sports bar/lounge. Strategically installed by Invictus throughout these and other spaces are 39 wall-mounted LG OLED TVs ranging from 65 to 83 inches, with 11 dedicated to the sports lounge alone. One of these TVs isn’t a TV at all—but a custom-designed Digital Projection dvLED video wall that delivers an immersive, cinematic experience unlike anything else in Natick, MA.
...
“Everyone has seen video from a projector, but few have experienced the stunning brightness, unbelievable color, contrast and pin-sharp clarity of images on something that looks like a TV, just on a much grander, more impressive scale. Digital Projection’s approach of powering the wall via Common Cathode technology makes the installation all the more impressive as it generates far less heat than other manufacturer designs,” said Invictus president Derek Bettencourt. “Eye-catching and visible from the second-floor entrance, it draws people in—and for a groundbreaking new business like Bosse, that kind of impact is invaluable.”
...
The entire Bosse Pickledom is a masterclass in integrated AV design. From Sonance PRO Series pendant speakers that fill the courts with energetic background music, to a high-performance Ubiquiti Wi-Fi network, intelligent door controls for secure access, and more than 150 strategically placed surveillance cameras, every square foot has been meticulously planned. Whether it's members enjoying spa-inspired locker rooms or casual players popping in for a quick match, the facility delivers a seamless, high-end experience from start to finish. With the push of a single button, staff can trigger pre-programmed AV and lighting scenes—like “Game Day” or the crowd-favorite “Glow-in-the-Dark Pickleball” on Friday nights, where black lights, pulse-pounding music, and live DJ sets transform the courts into an electrifying nightclub-style arena.
...
Certainly, the video wall was a serious investment—but one that immediately paid off in visual impact, customer engagement, and long-term flexibility. In a venue built on redefining what a pickleball facility can be, the Digital Projection LED video wall serves as both a conversation piece and a centerpiece—bright, bold, and brilliantly executed. With the success of the Bosse Pickledom, plans are already underway for expansion, including new facilities in Boston and Buffalo, the latter of which will feature a 60-foot-wide video wall—a testament to the client’s belief in large-format LED displays and in Digital Projection and Invictus Technology Solution’s ability to deliver them.

## 🎯 Project Overview

LawnTech Dynamics is an innovative multi-floor racquet sports facility concept combining autonomous operations, sustainable grass cultivation, and AI-powered performance analytics. Located in Naperville, Illinois, this facility aims to revolutionize indoor sports through cutting-edge technology and sustainable practices.

### Core Innovation
- **🌱 Autonomous Grass Management**: Vertical farming system that grows and swaps court surfaces robotically
- **🤖 AI-Powered Operations**: Self-managing facility with minimal human oversight
- **📊 Performance Analytics**: Real-time biomechanics tracking and injury prevention
- **♻️ Sustainable Design**: Solar-powered with advanced resource optimization

- Grass courts (replaceable modular turf)
- Hard courts
- Clay courts
- Wood courts
- Pro shop and premium locker rooms

### **First Floor** - Mezzanine Sports
- 16 badminton courts
- 4 squash courts
- 16 table tennis stations

### **Second Floor** - Specialty Courts
- 8 pickleball courts
- 1 historic real tennis court

### **Third Floor** - Vertical Grass Lab
2,000 m² autonomous farming facility with:
- Hydroponics and climate control
- Robotic patch transport system
- 60-minute court surface replacement capability

You integrate your Ditto instance with external messaging services -- such as

...
A connection represents a communication channel that uses a transport protocol to transmit
[Ditto Protocol](protocol-overview.html) messages. Ditto supports one-way and two-way communication,
enabling consumer/producer scenarios as well as full command-and-response workflows.

All connections are configured and supervised by Ditto's
[Connectivity service](architecture-services-connectivity.html).

filters to verify that a device only modifies its own

a verified device identity

.html)

* **address** -- interpreted as a queue, topic, etc. depending on the [connection type](#supported-connection-types)

Yes—but the exact intersection is rare. Most public examples are either a visual/operational digital twin or an autonomous booking-and-access system, not both.

Best matches:

- [LawnTech / ACE live demo](https://kvnloo.github.io/ace/) — the closest exact match: an interactive multi-floor racket-sports facility with tennis, badminton, squash, table tennis, pickleball, an autonomous grass lab, and an operations dashboard. The [MIT-licensed source](https://github.com/kvnloo/ace) uses React and Three.js and describes an Eclipse Ditto/OpenTwins architecture. Important caveat: this is a concept/prototype; its telemetry and autonomous systems should not be treated as evidence of a deployed physical facility.

- [Voltage Padel / Apollo3D](https://www.apollo3d.co.uk/facilities/) — a real padel-facility application using 360° CGI, drone mapping and Matterport-style twins to test layouts and finishes before opening. This is closer to design, construction documentation and marketing than a live operational twin. The specific Voltage Padel case is documented by [UK Tech News](https://uktechnews.co.uk/2026/06/30/leeds-tech-firm-on-the-ball-with-expansion-plans-as-padel-craze-sweeps-the-uk/).

- [Rafa Nadal Academy virtual world](https://imascono.com/en/rafa-nadal-academy/) — a large, multi-building virtual recreation covering over 76,000 m², including tennis and padel courts, hotel, school, sports centre and museum. It demonstrates multi-zone racket-sports visualization well, but is a gamified virtual tour rather than a sensor-connected operational twin.

- [St. Louis CITY SC stadium twin](https://www.wwt.com/video/wwt-digital-twin-st-louis-city-sc-energizer-park) — probably the strongest public demonstration of the operational layer you would want. It is built from BIM in Unreal Engine, supports 2D/VR interfaces, venue planning and operations, and models more than 300,000 controllable lights. It is football rather than racket sports, but technically more substantial than most court-facility examples.

- [OnePlan VenueTwin](https://www.oneplan.io/venue-twin/) — an interactive venue twin for scenario planning, security, workforce, hospitality and signage. Useful as a reference for floor/zone navigation and operational planning, although the public material is a product demonstration rather than an open implementation.

For genuinely autonomous facilities:

- [Pickleball 365 case study](https://podplay.app/blog/pickleball-365-a-podplay-case-study) — a physical, three-court facility operating 24/7 without a front desk. PodPlay handles booking, payment, app-based door access, scoreboards, video replay and remote monitoring. This is a strong operational reference, but not a spatial digital twin.

- [Urban Pickleball](https://www.playbypoint.com/customer-story/how-urban-pickleball-runs-a-fully-autonomous-club-in-downtown-seattle/) — an autonomous indoor Seattle club using app-based reservations, RemoteLock/PDK access, virtual check-in, waivers, lockers and merchandise management.

- [Doinsport autonomous padel](https://doinsport.com/en/autonomous-padel-tennis-courts) — demonstrates the complete unattended journey: booking, payment, temporary QR/PIN access and reservation-controlled lighting.

- [PickleTile Autonomous](https://pickletile.com/autonomous/) — integrates doors, kiosks, cameras, reservations, scoreboards, lighting and monitoring through PodPlay. This is particularly relevant if “autonomous” includes court-side media and security infrastructure.

Useful open-source building blocks:

- [OpenTwins](https://github.com/ertis-research/OpenTwins) — compositional twins, predicted/simulated data and Eclipse Ditto integration. Its maintainers explicitly label it under development.
- [Eclipse Ditto](https://github.com/eclipse-ditto/ditto) — device/twin state, authorization, messaging and commands.
- [OpenTwins Grafana frontend](https://github.com/ertis-research/grafana-app-opentwins) — twin management and monitoring through Grafana.
- [Smart Stadium Operations AI](https://github.com/rroshan-cell/smart-stadium-operations-ai) — a niche open-source simulated venue command centre with crowd, incident and evacuation scenarios; it also has a [public demo](https://smart-stadium-operations-ai-1.onrender.com).

The strongest composite reference is therefore: use ACE for the multi-floor racket-sports experience, the WWT stadium twin for BIM-linked operations, and Pickleball 365/PodPlay for proven unattended operation. I did not find a publicly verifiable physical multi-floor racket facility that exposes all three—live spatial twin, real telemetry/control and autonomous customer operation—in one public demo.

results.stdout:
The closest exact public view is GitHub’s commit search:

`https://github.com/search?q=author%3AYOUR_USERNAME&type=commits`

For example: [commits authored by `torvalds`](https://github.com/search?q=author%3Atorvalds&type=commits). This searches commit authorship rather than profile events, so stars and ordinary fork/bookmark activity are excluded. GitHub also supports repository, organization, date, and merge filters; see the [commit-search documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/search-github/searching-on-github/searching-commits) and [`gh search commits`](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_search_commits).

Caveats:

- It is a dynamic GitHub search page, not a static build log.
- Results depend on GitHub associating the commit’s author email with the account.
- GitHub profile contribution pages are not equivalent: GitHub counts repository creation, forks, issues, PRs, reviews, discussions, and qualifying commits as contributions. See [GitHub’s contribution criteria](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/reference/profile-contributions-reference).

I could not find a mature hosted service that simultaneously provides:

1. a static public page,
2. activity across multiple repositories,
3. strict commit-author filtering, and
4. no stars, bookmark forks, PRs, or other GitHub events.

Most nearby products—such as [BuilderLog](https://github.com/search?q=BuilderLog&type=repositories), [OSCT](https://osct.onrender.com/), and activity widgets—mix commits with PRs, issues, releases, or other events.

For a genuinely static version, the most reliable approach is a small GitHub Pages repository whose scheduled Action runs something like:

```sh
gh search commits "author:YOUR_USERNAME" \
  --sort author-date \
  --order desc \
  --limit 100 \
  --json sha,commit,repository,url
```

Then render that JSON into HTML, Markdown, or Atom and deploy it through [GitHub Pages](https://docs.github.com/en/pages) using [GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/using-custom-workflows-with-github-pages). That gives you an auditable, static, commit-authorship-only build log—the exact combination existing activity-feed products generally do not provide.

The closest exact public view is GitHub’s commit search:

`https://github.com/search?q=author%3AYOUR_USERNAME&type=commits`

For example: [commits authored by `torvalds`](https://github.com/search?q=author%3Atorvalds&type=commits). This searches commit authorship rather than profile events, so stars and ordinary fork/bookmark activity are excluded. GitHub also supports repository, organization, date, and merge filters; see the [commit-search documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/search-github/searching-on-github/searching-commits) and [`gh search commits`](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_search_commits).

Caveats:

- It is a dynamic GitHub search page, not a static build log.
- Results depend on GitHub associating the commit’s author email with the account.
- GitHub profile contribution pages are not equivalent: GitHub counts repository creation, forks, issues, PRs, reviews, discussions, and qualifying commits as contributions. See [GitHub’s contribution criteria](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/reference/profile-contributions-reference).

I could not find a mature hosted service that simultaneously provides:

1. a static public page,
2. activity across multiple repositories,
3. strict commit-author filtering, and
4. no stars, bookmark forks, PRs, or other GitHub events.

Most nearby products—such as [BuilderLog](https://github.com/search?q=BuilderLog&type=repositories), [OSCT](https://osct.onrender.com/), and activity widgets—mix commits with PRs, issues, releases, or other events.

For a genuinely static version, the most reliable approach is a small GitHub Pages repository whose scheduled Action runs something like:

```sh
gh search commits "author:YOUR_USERNAME" \
  --sort author-date \
  --order desc \
  --limit 100 \
  --json sha,commit,repository,url
```

Then render that JSON into HTML, Markdown, or Atom and deploy it through [GitHub Pages](https://docs.github.com/en/pages) using [GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/using-custom-workflows-with-github-pages). That gives you an auditable, static, commit-authorship-only build log—the exact combination existing activity-feed products generally do not provide.

Yes—this pattern exists, though it’s still niche. Strong public examples:

- **Aria Han** — probably the most agent-oriented implementation:
  [llms.txt](https://ariaxhan.com/llms.txt) · [projects.json](https://ariaxhan.com/api/projects.json)  
  Also publishes an [agent card](https://ariaxhan.com/.well-known/agent-card.json), [agent-skills index](https://ariaxhan.com/.well-known/agent-skills/index.json), and MCP endpoint.

- **Kevin Astuhuaman** — polished recruiting/product portfolio:
  [llms.txt](https://portfolio.kevinastuhuaman.com/llms.txt) · [projects.json](https://portfolio.kevinastuhuaman.com/projects.json) · [source repository](https://github.com/kevinastuhuaman/recruiting-portfolio)  
  The manifest includes summaries, canonical case-study links, and additional evidence/profile JSON.

- **Colin Zhou** — engineering portfolio with an MCP server:
  [llms.txt](https://czhou578.github.io/v3/llms.txt) · [projects.json](https://czhou578.github.io/v3/projects.json) · [GitHub profile](https://github.com/czhou578)  
  The agent guide explicitly points to structured projects, résumé Markdown, an FAQ, and MCP tools.

- **Angshuman Gupta** — product-leadership portfolio:
  [llms.txt](https://angshumangupta.com/llms.txt) · [projects.json](https://angshumangupta.com/api/projects.json)  
  Also exposes JSON endpoints for experience, articles, games, search, and site navigation.

- **Filippi Araujo** — developer/digital-garden hybrid:
  [llms.txt](https://www.filippiaraujo.com/llms.txt) · [projects.json](https://www.filippiaraujo.com/api/projects.json)  
  Particularly interesting because it also publishes writing, knowledge, resources, and a content-connection graph as JSON.

- **Daito** — creative-development portfolio with an explicit machine manifest:
  [llms.txt](https://daito.ws/llms.txt) · [manifest.json](https://daito.ws/api/manifest.json) · [projects.json](https://daito.ws/api/projects.json)  
  This is an especially literal match for “JSON manifest plus project feed.”

- **Florian Pellet / Minifolio** — niche open-source implementation:
  [source repository](https://github.com/sheraff/minifolio)  
  It dynamically serves `/llms.txt` and exposes project metadata through `/api/projects`; useful as implementation inspiration even though its project feed is an API route rather than a root-level manifest.

For the convention itself, [`llms.txt`](https://llmstxt.org/) is only a proposed discovery/index format; it does **not** prescribe a JSON project schema. The best implementations therefore link the JSON endpoint directly from `llms.txt` and make each record self-describing—typically `id`, `title`, `summary`, `status`, `technologies`, canonical URL, source/demo links, evidence, and `lastModified`.

# Agent Reach — 互联网能力路由器

15 平台、多后端。**本 skill 存在时必须用它访问这些平台，不要自己发明方案。**

## 常驻规则（全程适用）

1. **动手前先体检**：多后端/登录态平台（小红书/Reddit/B站/Twitter/Facebook/Instagram）先跑
   `agent-reach doctor --json`，按各平台 `active_backend` 字段选命令组。
2. **声明你在用什么**：开始干活前说一句「使用 agent-reach 的 X 平台 / Y 后端」。
3. **失败按 references 里的重试链处理**，不要瞎猜命令。
4. **全网调研类任务**：组合多平台（Exa 搜索 + Twitter/Reddit 看讨论 + 小红书/B站看中文场景），并行收集再汇总。
5. **替用户盯版本**：完成一次较大的调研/多平台任务后，顺手跑
   `agent-reach check-update`（很快，一个 API 调用）。有新版就在收尾汇报里附一句：
   「Agent Reach 有新版 vX.Y.Z，复制这句话给我即可更新：帮我更新 Agent Reach：
   https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Panniantong/agent-reach/main/docs/update.md」。
   不要中断当前任务去更新，也不要重复提醒同一个版本。

The llms.txt file spec is for files located in the root path`/llms.txt` of a website (or, optionally, in a subpath). A file following the spec contains the following sections as markdown, in the specific order:
...
- An optional byte-order mark (BOM)

- A blockquote with a short summary of the project, containing key information necessary for understanding the rest of the file
- Zero or more markdown sections (e.g. paragraphs, lists, etc) of any type except headings, containing more detailed information about the project and how to interpret the provided files
- Zero or more markdown sections delimited by H2 headers, containing “file lists” of URLs where further detail is available
- - Each “file list” is a markdown list, containing a required markdown hyperlink`[name](url)`, then optionally a`:` and notes about the file.

llms.txt is designed to coexist with current web standards. Because the format is lightweight, it adapts to many scenarios: developer portals, policy libraries, personal portfolios, online stores, academic handbooks, civic information, and more. The nbdev toolchain now renders Markdown versions of every page by default, so projects built with it inherit these benefits automatically.
...
Markdown remains the most LLM-friendly content format, and the`llms.txt` spec takes advantage of that familiarity. Files that follow the spec sit at the root of a site, or at the root of a dedicated sub-path, and present their content in the following order:
...
- H1 heading: the name of the project, product, or organization (required).
- Blockquote summary: a single-sentence synopsis that sets the context for everything else.
- Supporting context: one or more paragraphs, lists, or callouts that expand on how the site is organized or how to use the manifest. Additional headings are not allowed in this segment.
- File groups: zero or more sections introduced by`##` headings. Each section contains a Markdown list of links formatted as`[Name](URL)` with optional descriptions introduced by`:`.
...
## Optional`
...
consumers may safely skip those entries when building a smaller context window.
...
Because of that focus, the manifest often highlights Markdown versions of key pages, external resources such as official API references, and other context that would never appear in a traditional sitemap. It is primarily an inference-time asset today, though widespread adoption could influence future training datasets as well.

  [source repository](https://github.com/sheraff/minifolio)

For the convention itself, [`llms.txt`](https://llmstxt.org/) is only a proposed discovery/index format; it does **not** prescribe a JSON project schema. results.stdout:
Yes. I’d build this as three loosely coupled layers with one shared work/run schema.

## Recommended open stack

| Layer | Primary choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Company issue system | [Plane](https://github.com/makeplane/plane) | Self-hosted, human-friendly issues, cycles, projects, APIs |
| Dependency graph / agent queue | [Beads](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads) | Dependency-aware work graph, ready-work queries, agent-oriented CLI and structured output |
| Graph TUI | [Beads Viewer](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/beads_viewer) | DAG, critical path, PageRank, Kanban, and machine-readable “robot” mode |
| Repository instructions | [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/) | Portable repository-level instructions recognized across coding agents |
| Tool contracts | [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) | Standard boundary between harnesses and tools/data |
| Agent delegation | [A2A Protocol](https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A) | Agent discovery, task lifecycle, streaming, artifacts, cancellation |
| Client/harness boundary | [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com/) | Decouples terminal/editor clients from agent implementations |
| Durable orchestration | [Temporal](https://github.com/temporalio/temporal) | Retries, cancellation, timeouts, durable long-running execution |
| Agent session cockpit | [Agent Deck](https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck) | tmux TUI spanning Codex, Claude, Gemini, OpenCode and others |
| Worktree-oriented alternative | [dmux](https://github.com/standardagents/dmux) | Creates isolated worktrees, launches agents, merges results or opens PRs |
| Fleet-heavy alternative | [NTM](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm) | tmux control plane with multi-agent coordination and automation surfaces |
| Telemetry | [OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) | Vendor-neutral traces and metrics for model/agent operations |

### My concrete recommendation

Use:

```text
Plane ──sync/events──► normalized company graph
                         │
                         ├──► Beads per repository
                         ├──► Beads Viewer
                         └──► agent work-order API
                                  │
                         Temporal or a small queue
                                  │
                    Codex / Claude / OpenCode / CI agents
                                  │
                 MCP tools + A2A task/result envelopes
                                  │
                       Agent Deck or dmux cockpit
```

Plane should own company-visible status, assignment and planning. Beads should own fine-grained implementation dependencies and “what is unblocked?” inside repositories. Do not make both independently writable for the same status fields; define an explicit synchronization authority.

## The graph model

Keep the canonical model small:

```text
Nodes:
  initiative, project, issue, repository, service, document,
  pull_request, deployment, agent, run

Edges:
  parent_of, blocks, depends_on, implements, changes,
  documents, owned_by, assigned_to, produced_by
```

Every agent run should point to exactly one work item, while being allowed to discover new issues. Store lifecycle changes as append-only events and project the current graph from them.

I would initially use PostgreSQL tables plus recursive CTEs—not a dedicated graph database. Add something like [Apache AGE](https://github.com/apache/age) only if arbitrary multi-hop organizational queries become important.

## Harness contracts

AGENTS.md is useful guidance, but it is not a sufficiently strict execution contract. Add versioned JSON Schemas for three envelopes:

```json
{
  "work_order": {
    "id": "ENG-431",
    "objective": "Add resumable uploads",
    "scope": ["packages/uploader/**"],
    "constraints": ["do not change public API"],
    "acceptance": ["make test-uploader passes"],
    "permissions": ["repo.read", "repo.write", "tests.execute"],
    "deadline": "2026-08-02T18:00:00Z"
  }
}
```

```json
{
  "run_event": {
    "run_id": "run_123",
    "sequence": 17,
    "type": "waiting_for_approval",
    "timestamp": "...",
    "payload": {}
  }
}
```

```json
{
  "result": {
    "status": "completed",
    "summary": "...",
    "artifacts": [{"type": "git_commit", "ref": "..."}],
    "verification": [{"command": "make test-uploader", "exit_code": 0}],
    "discovered_work": [],
    "risks": []
  }
}
```

Use MCP for access to repositories, issue data and company systems. Use A2A only when one independently deployed agent delegates to another; it is unnecessary overhead for ordinary function calls. Wrap long-running runs in Temporal when losing a process or restarting a worker must not lose the task state.

## Terminal cockpit

For an immediately usable setup:

- Run sessions through [Agent Deck](https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck).
- Show the work graph through [Beads Viewer](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/beads_viewer).
- Use [lazygit](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit) for branch, diff and merge inspection.
- Put those three surfaces in a tmux layout.
- Use a worktree per active write-capable agent.

If worktree creation and merging are the dominant workflow, choose [dmux](https://github.com/standardagents/dmux) instead of Agent Deck. If you expect a larger terminal fleet with scripted coordination, evaluate [NTM](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm).

The cockpit’s top-level views should be:

1. Ready: unblocked issues ranked by priority and downstream impact.
2. Running: agent, issue, worktree, elapsed time and context usage.
3. Attention: approvals, failures, merge conflicts and stalled runs.
4. Graph: critical path and newly introduced blockers.
5. Delivery: PR, CI, review and deployment state.

## Niche projects worth examining

- [issue-graph](https://github.com/shdennlin/issue-graph): a small, read-only issue dependency visualizer with a pluggable-source architecture. Useful as reference code for a company graph UI.
- [DevBoard](https://github.com/FrancoisDuquesne/devboard): GitHub/GitLab merge requests, issues and todos presented as an interactive dependency graph.
- [muxa](https://github.com/Open330/muxa): tmux agent observability, attention routing, timelines and an MCP control plane.
- [Agent Tmux Manager](https://github.com/damellp/agent-tmux-manager): live agent state, costs, terminal capture and tmux layouts.
- [recon](https://github.com/gavraz/recon): a lighter Claude-focused tmux supervisor.
- [itsaplan](https://github.com/croffasia/itsaplan): experimental self-hosted tracker where agents are first-class assignees and are exposed through REST, MCP and webhooks.

My default starting point would be **Plane + Beads + AGENTS.md/MCP contracts + Agent Deck**, adding Temporal and A2A only once runs cross process or organizational boundaries. The niche projects are promising, but I’d pin versions and avoid making their internal schemas your company’s permanent contract.

2. **声明你在用什么**：开始干活前说一句「使用 agent-reach 的 X 平台 / Y 后端」。
3. **失败按 references 里的重试链处理**，不要瞎猜命令。

5. **替用户盯版本**：完成一次较大的调研/多平台任务后，顺手跑
   `agent-reach check-update`（很快，一个 API 调用）。有新版就在收尾汇报里附一句：
   「Agent Reach 有新版 vX.Y.Z，复制这句话给我即可更新：帮我更新 Agent Reach：
   https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Panniantong/agent-reach/main/docs/update.md」。

### Socket Isolation (v1.7.50+)
...
Run agent-deck on its own tmux server so it never touches your interactive tmux's config, bindings, or sessions. Opt-in via a single config line:
...
With this set, every agent-deck session is spawned as `tmux -L agent-deck …` — a fully isolated tmux server whose socket lives at `$TMUX_TMPDIR/tmux- /agent-deck` (or `/tmp/tmux- /agent-deck` when `TMUX_TMPDIR` is unset, the standard tmux fallback). Your regular tmux server at `default` is never touched.
...
**Default behavior unchanged.** Leave `socket_name` unset (the default) and agent-deck behaves exactly like v1.7.46: it uses your default tmux server. This is a pure opt-in.
...
**What socket isolation does not cover.** `socket_name` isolates agent-deck from *other* tmux servers on the host — a `tmux kill-server` in your shell, a stray `set-option -g` from your personal config, or an interactive session competing for the same socket. It does **not** harden agent-deck's own tmux server against bugs inside tmux itself. If agent-deck's internal session churn trips a tmux bug (for example, a control-mode race in older tmux builds), that failure happens on the isolated socket just as it would on the default one. The isolation boundary is "other tmux instances," not "all possible tmux crashes." Keep your tmux up to date alongside agent-deck.
...
**Per-session override.** The `agent-deck add` and `agent-deck launch` commands both accept `--tmux-socket ` to override the installation-wide default for one session:

## FAQ

 
 How is this different from just using tmux? 

Agent Deck adds AI-specific intelligence on top of tmux: smart status detection (knows when Claude is thinking vs. waiting), session forking with context inheritance, MCP management, global search across conversations, and organized groups. Think of it as tmux plus AI awareness.

 

 
 Can I use it on Windows? 

Yes, via WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux). [Install WSL](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install), then run the installer inside WSL. WSL2 is recommended for full feature support including MCP socket pooling.

 

 
 Can I use different Claude accounts/configs per profile?

 Will it interfere with my existing tmux setup? 

No. Agent Deck creates its own tmux sessions with the prefix `agentdeck_*`. Your existing sessions are untouched. The installer backs up your `~/.tmux.conf` before adding optional config, and you can skip it with `--skip-tmux-config`.

# Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol Specification
...
The Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol is an open standard designed to facilitate communication and interoperability between independent, potentially opaque AI agent systems. In an ecosystem where agents might be built using different frameworks, languages, or by different vendors, A2A provides a common language and interaction model.
...
This document provides the detailed technical specification for the A2A protocol. Its primary goal is to enable agents to:
...
- Discover each other's capabilities.
- Negotiate interaction modalities (text, files, structured data).
- Manage collaborative tasks.
- Securely exchange information to achieve user goals **without needing access to each other's internal state, memory, or tools.**
...
- **Interoperability:** Bridge the communication gap between disparate agentic systems.
- **Collaboration:** Enable agents to delegate tasks, exchange context, and work together on complex user requests.
- **Discovery:** Allow agents to dynamically find and understand the capabilities of other agents.
- **Flexibility:** Support various interaction modes including synchronous request/response, streaming for real-time updates, and asynchronous push notifications for long-running tasks.
- **Security:** Facilitate secure communication patterns suitable for enterprise environments, relying on standard web security practices.
- **Asynchronicity:** Natively support long-running tasks and interactions that may involve human-in-the-loop scenarios.
...
This specification is organized into three distinct layers that work together to provide a complete protocol definition:
...
**Layer 1: Canonical Data Model** defines the core data structures and message formats that all A2A implementations must understand. These are protocol agnostic definitions expressed as Protocol Buffer messages.
...
**Layer 2: Abstract Operations** describes the fundamental capabilities and behaviors that A2A agents must support, independent of how they are exposed over specific protocols.
...
**Layer 3: Protocol Bindings** provides concrete mappings of the abstract operations and data structures to specific protocol bindings (JSON-RPC, gRPC, HTTP/REST), including method names, endpoint patterns, and protocol-specific behaviors.
...
In addition to the protocol requirements defined in this document, the file `spec/a2a.proto` is the single authoritative normative definition of all protocol data objects and request/response messages. A generated JSON artifact (`spec/a2a.json`, produced at build time and not committed) MAY be published for convenience to tooling and the website, but it is a non-normative build artifact. SDK language bindings, schemas, and any other derived forms **MUST** be regenerated from the proto (directly or via code generation) rather than edited manually.
...

- **A2A Server (Remote Agent):** An agent or agentic system that exposes an A2A-compliant endpoint, processing tasks and providing responses.
...
- **Agent Card:** A JSON metadata document published by an A2A Server, describing its identity, capabilities, skills, service endpoint, and authentication requirements.
...
- **Task:** The fundamental unit of work managed by A2A, identified by a unique ID. Tasks are stateful and progress through a defined lifecycle.
...

## 4. Protocol Data Model
...
The A2A protocol defines a canonical data model using Protocol Buffers. All protocol bindings **MUST** provide functionally equivalent representations of these data structures.

When a task update occurs, the agent sends an HTTP POST request to the configured webhook URL. The payload uses the same [`StreamResponse`](#323-stream-response) format as streaming operations, allowing push notifications to deliver the same event types as real-time streams.

Extensions allow agents to declare additional capabilities such as protocol enhancements or vendor-specific features, maintain compatibility with clients that don't support specific extensions, enable innovation through experimental or domain-specific features without modifying the core protocol, and facilitate standardization by providing a pathway for community-developed features to become part of the core specification.

contract compilation, skill discovery, and decision gating for free.

                 │  newline-delimited JSON, child stdio
                 ▼

 load only on demand.
3. **Decision** — gate work through the

...
Returns only the verification gates — the named checklists and shell commands

...
The Consensus Hardening Protocol **R0 gate**: the cheapest, highest-leverage

A one-shot adversarial pass for high-stakes changes: CHP attacks the claim's

Author: N/A
Highlights:
Today, we’re launching a new, open protocol called Agent2Agent (A2A), with support and contributions from more than 50 technology partners like Atlassian, Box, Cohere, Intuit, Langchain, MongoDB, PayPal, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, UKG and Workday; and leading service providers including Accenture, BCG, Capgemini, Cognizant, Deloitte, HCLTech, Infosys, KPMG, McKinsey, PwC, TCS, and Wipro. The A2A protocol will allow AI agents to communicate with each other, securely exchange information, and coordinate actions on top of various enterprise platforms or applications. We believe the A2A framework will add significant value for customers, whose AI agents will now be able to work across their entire enterprise application estates.
...
A2A is an open protocol that complements Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP), which provides helpful tools and context to agents. Drawing on Google's internal expertise in scaling agentic systems, we designed the A2A protocol to address the challenges we identified in deploying large-scale, multi-agent systems for our customers. A2A empowers developers to build agents capable of connecting with any other agent built using the protocol and offers users the flexibility to combine agents from various providers. Critically, businesses benefit from a standardized method for managing their agents across diverse platforms and cloud environments. We believe this universal interoperability is essential for fully realizing the potential of collaborative AI agents.
...
A2A is an open protocol that provides a standard way for agents to collaborate with each other, regardless of the underlying framework or vendor. While designing the protocol with our partners, we adhered to five key principles:
...
A2A facilitates communication between a "client" agent and a “remote” agent. A client agent is responsible for formulating and communicating tasks, while the remote agent is responsible for acting on those tasks in an attempt to provide the correct information or take the correct action. This interaction involves several key capabilities:
...
- Capability discovery: Agents can advertise their capabilities using an “Agent Card” in JSON format, allowing the client agent to identify the best agent that can perform a task and leverage A2A to communicate with the remote agent.
...
- Task management: The communication between a client and remote agent is oriented towards task completion, in which agents work to fulfill end-user requests. This “task” object is defined by the protocol and has a lifecycle. It can be completed immediately or, for long-running tasks, each of the agents can communicate to stay in sync with each other on the latest status of completing a task. The output of a task is known as an “artifact.”
...
- Collaboration: Agents can send each other messages to communicate context, replies, artifacts, or user instructions.
...
- User experience negotiation: Each message includes “parts,” which is a fully formed piece of content, like a generated image. Each part has a specified content type, allowing client and remote agents to negotiate the correct format needed and explicitly include negotiations of the user’s UI capabilities–e.g., iframes, video, web forms, and more.
...
We’re committed to building the protocol in collaboration with our partners and the community in the open. We’re releasing the protocol as open source and setting up clear pathways for contribution.
...
Review the full specification draft, try out code samples, and see example scenarios on the A2A website and learn how you can contribute.
...

Use:

Nodes:
  initiative, project, issue, repository, service, document,
  pull_request, deployment, agent, run

Edges:
  parent_of, blocks, depends_on, implements, changes,
  documents, owned_by, assigned_to, produced_by
```

Every agent run should point to exactly one work item, while being allowed to discover new issues. Store lifecycle changes as append-only events and project the current graph from them.

I would initially use PostgreSQL tables plus recursive CTEs—not a dedicated graph database. Add something like [Apache AGE](https://github.com/apache/age) only if arbitrary multi-hop organizational queries become important.

## Harness contracts

AGENTS.md is useful guidance, but it is not a sufficiently strict execution contract. Add versioned JSON Schemas for three envelopes:

```json
{
  "work_order": {
    "id": "ENG-431",
    "objective": "Add resumable uploads",
    "scope": ["packages/uploader/**"],
    "constraints": ["do not change public API"],
    "acceptance": ["make test-uploader passes"],
    "permissions": ["repo.read", "repo.write", "tests.execute"],
    "deadline": "2026-08-02T18:00:00Z"
  }
}
```

```json
{
  "run_event": {
    "run_id": "run_123",
    "sequence": 17,
    "type": "waiting_for_approval",
    "timestamp": "...",
    "payload": {}
  }
}
```

```json
{
  "result": {
    "status": "completed",
    "summary": "...",
    "artifacts": [{"type": "git_commit", "ref": "..."}],
    "verification": [{"command": "make test-uploader", "exit_code": 0}],
    "discovered_work": [],
    "risks": []
  }
}
```

Use MCP for access to repositories, issue data and company systems. Use A2A only when one independently deployed agent delegates to another; it is unnecessary overhead for ordinary function calls. Wrap long-running runs in Temporal when losing a process or restarting a worker must not lose the task state.

## Terminal cockpit

For an immediately usable setup:

- Run sessions through [Agent Deck](https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck).
- Show the work graph through [Beads Viewer](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/beads_viewer).
- Use [lazygit](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit) for branch, diff and merge inspection.
- Put those three surfaces in a tmux layout.
- Use a worktree per active write-capable agent.

If worktree creation and merging are the dominant workflow, choose [dmux](https://github.com/standardagents/dmux) instead of Agent Deck. If you expect a larger terminal fleet with scripted coordination, evaluate [NTM](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm).

The cockpit’s top-level views should be:

1. Ready: unblocked issues ranked by priority and downstream impact.
2. Running: agent, issue, worktree, elapsed time and context usage.
3. Attention: approvals, failures, merge conflicts and stalled runs.
4. Graph: critical path and newly introduced blockers.
5. Delivery: PR, CI, review and deployment state.

## Niche projects worth examining

- [issue-graph](https://github.com/shdennlin/issue-graph): a small, read-only issue dependency visualizer with a pluggable-source architecture. Useful as reference code for a company graph UI.
- [DevBoard](https://github.com/FrancoisDuquesne/devboard): GitHub/GitLab merge requests, issues and todos presented as an interactive dependency graph.
- [muxa](https://github.com/Open330/muxa): tmux agent observability, attention routing, timelines and an MCP control plane.
- [Agent Tmux Manager](https://github.com/damellp/agent-tmux-manager): live agent state, costs, terminal capture and tmux layouts.
- [recon](https://github.com/gavraz/recon): a lighter Claude-focused tmux supervisor.
- [itsaplan](https://github.com/croffasia/itsaplan): experimental self-hosted tracker where agents are first-class assignees and are exposed through REST, MCP and webhooks.

My default starting point would be **Plane + Beads + AGENTS.md/MCP contracts + Agent Deck**, adding Temporal and A2A only once runs cross process or organizational boundaries. The niche projects are promising, but I’d pin versions and avoid making their internal schemas your company’s permanent contract.

Who is Kevin Rajan?

./index.html:362:

Kevin Rajan (GitHub kvnloo, X @_kvnloo) is a builder, engineer, scientist, solutions architect, systems thinker, and automation orchestration expert — solo founder of zer0 who ships public software around agent tooling, health, world simulation, and autonomous development. This site is his chronological public commit archive, not a full private portfolio.

His public work focuses on using AI and code to increase individual agency—particularly through autonomous-development systems, agent tooling, health technology, and simulations.\n\nPublicly, he is known for:\n\n- AI-agent infrastructure and autonomous development\n - `tmux-agent-fleet`: a zero-daemon command palette for coordinating coding agents across tmux panes.\n - `evolve`: a multi-agent orchestration toolkit built around Claude Code agents.\n - Tools for agent monitoring, verification harnesses, and evidence-based “done” states.\n\n- `zerOS`\n - A stealth company-operating-system track under zer0.\n - Public components include issue-graph and scheduling infrastructure (`_pm`), a terminal cockpit, agent-harness contracts, and voice adapters.\n - The public description intentionally provides limited product detail.\n\n- Digital twins and interactive simulations\n - `ace`: a digital twin of an autonomous, multi-floor racket-sports facility.\n - Other public experiments include Three.js environments, generative art, 3D scene tooling, and infotainment-interface prototypes.\n\n- Health and human-performance technology\n - Health and peak performance are recurring themes in his stated mission and one of zer0’s public product tracks.\n\n- Earlier mobile and audio engineering\n - `AudioEngine`, dating to 2017, includes an iOS real-time noise meter and a 14-band dual-channel equalizer.\n\nHis canonical public build log currently catalogs 52 repositories from 2017–2026 where he authored at least one commit: 25 products, 18 experiments, and 9 professional projects. It deliberately excludes private repositories and forks he merely bookmarked, so it should be understood as a verified public-build archive—not a complete résumé or account of private work.\n\nSources:\n\n- Canonical build log and biography: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/\n- Machine-readable site guide: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/llms.txt\n- Public project manifest: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/data/manifest.json\n- GitHub profile: https://github.com/kvnloo\n- X: https://x.com/_kvnloo\n\nIn one sentence: Kevin Rajan is publicly known as an AI-focused builder creating agent orchestration tools, autonomous-development infrastructure, company-OS components, simulations, and human-performance technology under the zer0 umbrella.\n", ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T08-57-01/raw.json:23: "prompt": "What is zer0 in relation to Kevin Rajan / kvnloo?", ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T08-57-01/raw.json:24: "stdout": "“zer0” is Kevin Rajan’s umbrella company/build identity for the public work published under his GitHub handle, `kvnloo`.\n\nThe public hierarchy is:\n\n- Kevin Rajan — the builder/person\n- `kvnloo` — his GitHub identity\n- zer0 — the company-level umbrella used to organize his work\n- Products, experiments, and professional projects — the categories beneath zer0\n- zerOS — a specific stealth product within zer0, described publicly as a “company operating system” covering issues, agent harnesses, cockpit, and voice\n\nPublic zerOS components include `_pm`, `zer0-cockpit`, `zer0-harness-spine`, `zer0-voice`, and the early `z0` scaffold. Other zer0 work includes Evolve, health and world-simulation tracks, agent tooling, boplog, and various experiments.\n\nSo, in short: **zer0 is the umbrella; zerOS is one product under it; Kevin Rajan/kvnloo is the builder behind the public work.**\n\nSources:\n\n- Canonical build log: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/\n- Public hierarchy and exact taxonomy: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/data/hierarchy.json\n- Public-project manifest: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/data/manifest.json\n\nThe public sources label zer0 as a “company,” but they do not establish its legal structure, funding, staffing, or other private details.\n", ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T08-57-01/raw.json:32: "prompt_id": "product-boplog", ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T08-57-01/raw.json:33: "prompt": "What is boplog by Kevin Rajan / kvnloo?", ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T08-57-01/raw.json:34: "stdout": "Boplog is Kevin Rajan’s public build log: a static, data-driven, chronological archive of public GitHub repositories that `kvnloo` has actually committed to.\n\nIt:\n\n- Includes public repositories with at least one commit authored by Kevin.\n- Excludes private repositories and bookmark-only forks with no authored commits.\n- Classifies work under the `zer0` umbrella as product, experiment, or professional.\n- Covers public projects in areas such as agent tooling, autonomous development, health, world simulation, and zerOS.\n- Provides both a human-readable website and machine-readable JSON, Atom, OpenAPI, CLI, and MCP access.\n\nAs of the public data refresh dated July 31, 2026, the archive lists 52 projects spanning 2017–2026. It is a public commit archive—not a complete account of Kevin’s private work or unpublished roadmap.\n\nSources: [canonical boplog site](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/), [AI-readable guide](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/llms.txt), and [JSON manifest](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/data/manifest.json).\n", ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T08-57-01/raw.json:43: "prompt": "What is the evolve project associated with Kevin Rajan or kvnloo?", ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T08-57-01/raw.json:44: "stdout": "Evolve is Kevin Rajan’s public autonomous AI development and multi-agent orchestration project.\n\nIt combines several agent-development tools into one systematic workflow:\n\n- Claude Flow and SPARC for specification, architecture, TDD, and coordinated execution\n- CCPM for PRDs, issue decomposition, GitHub synchronization, and worktrees\n- SuperClaude for behavioral and research modes\n- Claude Squad for parallel agent sessions\n- Continuous Claude for iterative development and PR automation\n- Claude Code as the main execution engine\n\nIts central concept is C(RAID): Research → Analysis → Integration → Deployment → feedback, an AI-oriented alternative to a conventional code-first CI/CD cycle.\n\nThe canonical build-log record classifies Evolve as:\n\n- Company umbrella: zer0\n- Kind: product\n- Product: evolve\n- Blueprint track: 3\n- Category: dev\n- Primary language: Shell\n- Public-record date: December 2, 2025\n- License: MIT\n- Repository: https://github.com/kvnloo/evolve\n- Documentation: https://kvnloo.github.io/evolve/\n\nIn short, Evolve is intended as an end-to-end framework for autonomous software development in which specialized AI agents research, plan, implement, test, review, and manage delivery across isolated sessions.\n\nSources: [canonical boplog record](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/), [public Evolve documentation](https://kvnloo.github.io/evolve/), and [GitHub repository](https://github.com/kvnloo/evolve). These describe public work only and do not establish any private roadmap or deployment.\n", ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T08-57-01/raw.json:54: "stdout": "tmux-agent-fleet is kvnloo’s open-source tmux plugin for quickly finding, monitoring, and switching between coding-agent panes.\n\nIt turns `prefix + f` into a searchable `fzf` command palette that:\n\n- Discovers active agents directly from tmux process metadata—no daemon or agent hooks.\n- Supports Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, Grok, Oh My Pi, Pi, Fable, ordinary shells, and optional Agent Deck sessions.\n- Shows a live pane preview and jumps to the selected pane.\n- Avoids injecting commands, renaming sessions, managing worktrees, or sending telemetry.\n- Uses pywal colors when available, with built-in fallback styling.\n\nIt is a switcher and monitor, not an agent orchestrator. Because it is harness-neutral and hook-free, its activity indicator reflects pane activity rather than semantic states such as “waiting for permission.”\n\nPublic build-log fields classify it as:\n\n- Type: public, Shell\n- Category: dev\n- Company: zer0\n- Kind: product\n- Product: agent tooling\n- Public record date: July 14, 2026\n- License: MIT\n\nSources:\n- Canonical build log: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/\n- Repository: https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet\n", ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T08-57-01/raw.json:63: "prompt": "What is zerOS (zeros) in Kevin Rajan's public work?", ./data/llmeo/runs/2026-07-31T08-57-01/raw.json:64: "stdout": "In Kevin Rajan’s public work, zerOS is described as a stealth “company operating system” for zer0—not a conventional desktop or mobile OS.\n\nIts public architecture has four main parts:\n\n- Issues / project-management core: `_pm` — an issue graph, ledger, ticket scheduler, and benchmark system, published as a mirror of the company OS PM core.\n- Cockpit: `zer0-cockpit` — a read-only, dependency-free terminal dashboard showing explicit project progress.\n- Agent harness: `zer0-harness-spine` — minimal contracts and provider adapters for the Zer0 agent stack, deliberately excluding orchestration state.\n- Voice: `zer0-voice` — adapters connecting the harness to machine-wide speech services without bundling speech models.\n\nThe build log also associates `z0`, an early placeholder scaffold from 2025, with zerOS.\n\nSo, based strictly on the public record, zerOS appears to be an AI-assisted company execution layer: it represents work as issues and dependencies, schedules and benchmarks agent work, exposes progress through a cockpit, and supports voice interaction. An empty or absent\nfile means no panes matched (or the daemon isn't running).\n...\n### Daemon lifecycle — two ways to start\n...\nBoth methods rely on `--ensure-running`, which makes startup idempotent via a\nPID file at `~/.cache/twmux/watch.pid`. agent behavioral characteristics including agent type, model, system prompts, and focus patterns. NTM includes built-in profiles for common roles like architect, implementer, reviewer, tester, and documenter.\n\n| Command | Arguments | Description |\n|---------|-----------|-------------|\n| `ntm profiles list` | `[--agent TYPE] [--tag TAG] [--json]` | List available profiles |\n| `ntm profiles show` | ` [--json]` | Show detailed profile information |\n| `ntm personas list` | `[--agent TYPE] [--tag TAG] [--json]` | Alias for `profiles list` |\n| `ntm personas show` | ` [--json]` | Alias for `profiles show` |\n\n**Profile Sources (later overrides earlier):**\n1. **Built-in**: Compiled into NTM (architect, implementer, reviewer, tester, documenter)\n2. **User**: `~/.config/ntm/personas.toml`\n3. **Project**: `.ntm/personas.toml`\n\n**Profile Sets:**\n\nProfile sets are named groups of profiles for quick spawning:\n\n```toml\n# In ~/.config/ntm/personas.toml or .ntm/personas.toml\n[[persona_sets]]\nname = \"backend-team\"\ndescription = \"Full backend development team\"\npersonas = [\"architect\", \"implementer\", \"implementer\", \"tester\"]\n```\n\n**Examples:**\n\n```bash\nntm profiles list # List all profiles\nntm profiles list --agent claude # Filter by agent type\nntm profiles list --tag review # Filter by tag\nntm profiles list --json # JSON output for scripts\nntm profiles show architect # Show profile details\nntm profiles show architect --json # JSON output with source info\n```\n\n**Using Profiles with Spawn:**\n\n```bash\nntm spawn myproject --profiles=architect,implementer,tester\nntm spawn myproject --profile-set=backend-team\n```\n\n### AI Agent Integration (Robot Mode)\n\nNTM provides machine-readable output for integration with AI coding agents and automation pipelines. All robot commands output JSON by default and follow consistent exit codes (0=success, 1=error, 2=unavailable).\n\n**Robot Output Formats + Verbosity:**\n\n- `--robot-format=json|toon|auto` (Alias: `--robot-output-format=...`; Env: `NTM_ROBOT_FORMAT`, `NTM_OUTPUT_FORMAT`, `TOON_DEFAULT_FORMAT`; Config: `[robot.output] format` = json|toon). `auto` currently resolves to JSON.\n- `--robot-verbosity=terse|default|debug` (Env: `NTM_ROBOT_VERBOSITY`). Applies to JSON/TOON only.\n- Config default for verbosity: `~/.config/ntm/config.toml` → `[robot] verbosity = \"default\"`.\n- `--robot-terse` is a **separate single-line format** and ignores `--robot-format` / `--robot-verbosity`.\n- JSON remains the default. For scripts that must always get JSON, pass `--robot-format=json` (or `--robot-output-format=json`) explicitly.\n- TOON is token-efficient (often ~40-60% fewer tokens for tabular outputs) but only supports uniform arrays and simple objects; unsupported shapes return an error. Use `--robot-format=json` or `auto` to avoid TOON failures.\n\n**Example output (JSON vs TOON):**\n\nJSON (default; also `--robot-format=json`):\n\n```json\n{\n \"success\": true,\n \"timestamp\": \"2026-01-22T01:23:00Z\",\n \"sessions\": [\n {\"name\": \"myproject\", \"attached\": true, \"windows\": 1}\n ]\n}\n```\n\nTOON (e.g. `--robot-output-format=toon`):\n\n```text\nsuccess: true\ntimestamp: 2026-01-22T01:23:00Z\nsessions[1]{attached,name,windows}:\n true\tmyproject\t1\n```\n\n**Robot JSON Envelope Spec (v1.0.0):**\n\nAll robot outputs share a common envelope structure:\n\n| Field | Type | Required | Description |\n|-------|------|----------|-------------|\n| `success` | boolean | Yes | Whether the operation succeeded |\n| `timestamp` | string | Yes | RFC3339 timestamp (UTC) |\n| `version` | string | Yes | Envelope schema version (semver, currently \"1.0.0\") |\n| `output_format` | string | Yes | Output format used (\"json\" or \"toon\") |\n| `error` | string | No | Human-readable error message (on failure) |\n| `error_code` | string | No | Machine-parseable error code (e.g., \"SESSION_NOT_FOUND\") |\n| `hint` | string | No | Suggested remediation action |\n| `_meta` | object | No | Optional timing/debug metadata |\n\nThe `_meta` field (when present) contains:\n\n| Field | Type | Description |\n|-------|------|-------------|\n| `duration_ms` | integer | Command execution time in milliseconds |\n| `exit_code` | integer | Process exit code (0=success) |\n| `command` | string | The robot command that was executed |\n\nExample envelope:\n\n```json\n{\n \"success\": true,\n \"timestamp\": \"2026-01-27T07:00:00Z\",\n \"version\": \"1.0.0\",\n \"output_format\": \"json\",\n \"_meta\": {\n \"duration_ms\": 42,\n \"command\": \"robot-status\"\n },\n \"sessions\": [...]\n}\n```\n\n**State Inspection:**\n\n```bash\nntm --robot-status # Sessions, panes, agent states\nntm --robot-context=SESSION # Context window usage per agent\nntm --robot-snapshot # Unified state: sessions + beads + alerts + mail\nntm --robot-tail=SESSION # Recent pane output (--lines=50 --panes=1,2)\nntm --robot-inspect-pane=SESS # Detailed pane inspection (--inspect-index=N)\nntm --robot-files=SESSION # File changes with agent attribution (--files-window=15m)\nntm --robot-metrics=SESSION # Session metrics export (--metrics-period=24h)\nntm --robot-palette # Query command palette (--palette-category=NAME)\nntm --robot-plan # bv execution plan with parallelizable tracks\nntm --robot-graph # Dependency graph insights\nntm --robot-dashboard # Dashboard summary (markdown or --json)\nntm --robot-terse # Single-line encoded state (minimal tokens)\nntm --robot-markdown # System state as markdown tables\nntm --robot-health # Project health summary\nntm --robot-version # Version info\nntm --robot-help # Full robot mode documentation\n```\n\n**Agent Control:**\n\n```bash\nntm --robot-send=SESSION --msg=\"Fix auth\" --type=claude # Send to agents\nntm --robot-ack=SESSION --ack-timeout=30s # Watch for responses\nntm --robot-spawn=SESSION --spawn-cc=2 --spawn-wait # Create session\nntm --robot-interrupt=SESSION --interrupt-msg=\"Stop\" #
